title: Notes on the Song of Enlightenment
author: Zhanran (annotator)
excerpt: The Song of Enlightenment describes the dream of ignorance awakened — the realm in which, for example, the song says, "the dharmakāya awakened — not a single thing is there," "in the dream the six destinies are plainly there; once awakened, the great thousand worlds are empty and bare," and so on. The Song of Enlightenment shares with the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra, and the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch the same core: it teaches the realization and entry into the patience of the unborn, causing the self-nature to return to its original source.

Therefore readers should become familiar with the reality of all dharmas and with the self-nature and the intrinsic nature. On the reality of all dharmas, see
The Reality of All Dharmas

Mind, Intrinsic Nature, and the Tathagata-Store

[Patience of the unborn] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising. The dharma of non-arising means the true reality of all dharmas, which neither arises nor ceases; when true wisdom comes to rest upon this principle and never again retreats or falls away, this is called the "patience of the unborn."
The Buddha said:
"There is no sentient being who does not possess the Tathagata's wisdom, but because of false thinking

inverted and attached, they do not realize it. If they free themselves from false thinking, then the wisdom of all-knowing, the wisdom of spontaneity, and the unobstructed wisdom will appear before them."
(The Eighty-Fascicle Avatamsaka Sutra, fascicle 51, "The Appearance of the Tathagata," chapter 37, part 2)
The Song of Enlightenment
lays bare the profound meaning of Chan in its entirety, and

its verses are so fluent that one may easily awaken to the gist of the Buddhadharma while chanting them aloud. It is said that it was once transmitted to India under the title The Mahayana Sutra That Dispels Doubts, by the Sage of Cinasthana.
(This account
comes from Dahui Zonggao's Universal Discourses, Huihong Juefan's Night Talks in the Cold Studio, and Yanqi's own preface to his Remarks on the Song of Enlightenment, among others.

[The gist of the Buddhadharma] This, together with such phrases as "the First Patriarch's purpose in coming from the west," "the purpose of coming from the west," and "the Patriarch's purpose," all point to the profound meaning of the Buddhadharma and the true marrow of Chan. [The First Patriarch's purpose in coming from the west] The first patriarch of Chan, Bodhidharma, came from the western lands to the central land to transmit Chan; this is the mind-seal of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and it is called "the First Patriarch's purpose in coming from the west." [Mind-seal] "Mind" is the Buddha-mind; "seal" means to approve, to seal and to confirm. Chan does not establish words and does not rely on speech; it only transmits mind to mind, using the Buddha-mind to seal and confirm the minds of sentient beings and to realize the mark of non-duality.
[Cinasthana] In ancient India, China was called Cinasthana.
Tradition has always held

that the author of the Song of Enlightenment was Xuanjue, a native of Yongjia county in Wenzhou prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Mingdao, his religious name Zhenjue, his posthumous title "Master Without Marks," and he is known to the world as Master Yongjia. Present-day scholars have determined that the original author of the Song of Enlightenment
must
be
the great man who caused the Sixth Patriarch's Dharma to spread throughout the world,
Shenhui.

Do you not see the idle man of the Way, / who has nothing left to learn and nothing to do? / He clears no false thinking and seeks no truth. / The true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature; / the illusory empty body is itself the dharmakāya.

Do you see that man of the Way, so free of affairs, who neither learns nor acts? He neither removes delusion nor seeks the truth, for he has realized that the true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature, and that the true nature of the illusory physical body and of the dharmakāya are not two and not different.
"The true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is itself the dharmakāya" — this is the state of one who has realized the patience of the unborn.

[Do you not see] Do you see it? This phrase answers the last line of the piece, "If you have not understood, I now give you the formula," for this song is sung expressly for you, which makes the reader feel all the closer to it. The master's compassion fairly leaps off the page. [Nothing left to learn and nothing to do] Neither learning nor acting. [Idle man of the Way] A man of the Way with nothing to do, who does not create or stir up any karmic activity. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:

"One who has the patience of the unborn finds not even the subtlest dharma obtainable, much less a great one; this is called non-arising. Having attained this dharma of non-arising, one neither creates nor stirs up any karmic activity — this is called attaining the patience of the unborn."

[He does not rid himself of false thinking, nor does he seek the true] This is already the state of "abiding in nothing yet giving rise to mind, giving rise to mind yet abiding in nothing; the feelings of sage and ordinary being are extinguished, and the views of true and false are emptied." It belongs to the practice of guarding and letting be, and there the work of letting be has been accomplished. Therefore the floating clouds of the five aggregates and the water-bubbles of the three poisons can do him no harm; they merely come and go as emptiness, appear and vanish as illusion.

[Guarding and letting be] These are the two great stages of cultivating the Way. Guarding: cutting off thought and deliberation. Letting be: letting the mind be free and at ease, without love or hate, taking or rejecting. See
The Fourth Patriarch's Instruction to Farong
. [True nature] The nature that is real, that is, true reality (the actual state of things). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"Jian
(Xue Jian)
asked: What is the Mahayana view? The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)
answered: The ordinary person sees illumination and ignorance as two; the wise one understands that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is
true nature
(For the annotation, see
Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
) On true reality, see
The Reality of All Dharmas

. [The illusory empty body is itself the dharmakāya] The illusory physical body and the dharmakāya are alike illusions; as to their essential nature (true reality), the physical body and the dharmakāya are not two and not different. [The dharmakāya too is illusion] The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of the Original Nature says:
"Ever contemplate the wondrous dharmakāya of all Buddhas: its essential nature is like space and cannot be grasped."
The Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra says:
"The dharmakāya is like an illusion, a dream; how can it be praised? To know it is without nature and without arising — this alone is called praising the Buddha."
[Buddha-nature] The nature that is forever unchanging in all sentient beings and that can awaken and become Buddha. The Nirvana Sutra says:
"All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; the Tathagata abides forever without change."

Awakened to the dharmakāya, there is not a single thing; / the self-nature of the original source is the innate, natural Buddha. / The five aggregates are floating clouds that come and go in emptiness; / the three poisons are water-bubbles that appear and vanish in illusion.

Having realized the dharmakāya, one understands that all dharmas are illusions and that originally there is not a single thing; the self-nature (the intrinsic nature) of the original source is the innate Buddha. Therefore the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness), like floating clouds, come and go in emptiness, and the three poisons (greed, hatred, and delusion), like water-bubbles, appear and vanish in illusion, and neither can do one any harm.
[The innate Buddha] Another name for the dharmakāya Buddha. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:
"Patriarchs and Buddhas alike point to this mind and thereby accomplish Buddhahood; it is also called the innate Buddha, the dharmakāya Buddha, the nature Buddha, and the Buddha of Suchness."

[The five aggregates are floating clouds that come and go in emptiness; the three poisons are water-bubbles that appear and vanish in illusion] No longer driven and entangled by the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) or the three poisons (greed, hatred, and delusion). This is
the state of giving rise to mind without abiding

, which shows that the work of letting be has been accomplished. Yet for ordinary people the work of guarding is not yet accomplished, let alone the work of letting be; they are still driven and entangled by the five aggregates and the three poisons. How would they dare to say, "I rid myself of no false thinking and seek no truth"?

[Guarding and letting be] Guarding and letting be at ease: these are the two stages of purifying away habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. "Guarding" means caring for the holy embryo (the self-nature that has just begun to awaken) with all one's might, so that it suffers no harm from greed, hatred, and delusion, and thereby accomplishing the first two of the four patiencees (the patience of submission and the patience of gentle compliance); "letting be at ease" means that after the holy embryo has grown to adulthood, one follows circumstances and conditions and lets it function naturally, tempering it further amid favorable and adverse conditions, and thereby accomplishing the last two of the four patiencees (the patience of the unborn and the patience of quiescent extinction).

[The four patiencees] The patience of submission, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of the unborn, and the patience of quiescent extinction. The patience of submission: the beginner who wishes to bear with favorable and adverse conditions (without giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion) must first tame and subdue the mind. The patience of gentle compliance: when the mind has long been tamed and subdued, then on meeting conditions and circumstances one can endure naturally without forcing suppression (without giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion); at that time the mind is gentle and compliant. The patience of the unborn: one who has entered the stage of sagehood understands that all dharmas are from the outset unborn, that sentient and insentient alike are produced by conditions and are without nature, and that in their very substance they are empty; therefore within dharmas that are without nature the mind of patience is unmoved, and one personally realizes non-arising. The patience of quiescent extinction: the sage in the stage of fruition thoroughly realizes the quiescent realm of nirvāṇa, and both the marks of movement and of stillness accord with suchness. [Suchness] The realm of self-nature in which inverted discrimination does not arise. Because it is the tathatā (the true reality of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom of suchness, it is called "suchness."

[Realize true reality: no person, no dharma; / in a single instant the Avici karma is dissolved. / If with false words I should deceive living beings, / I would draw upon myself the tongue-pulling hell for kalpas of dust and sand.]

When one realizes the true reality of all dharmas, there is neither the attachment to a person nor the attachment to dharmas; the karmic consciousness of beginningless ignorance dissolves at once with the thought, and in a single instant the karma that would fall into the Avici hell is extinguished. If I were deceiving living beings with false words, I would be bringing upon myself the karma of the tongue-pulling hell for kalpas as numerous as dust and sand.
[True reality] The actual state of things, that is, the true reality of all dharmas (see
The Reality of All Dharmas

[Attachment to person] Also called attachment to self, or the person-self: falsely clinging to the body-and-mind falsely compounded of the five aggregates as "I." One who severs the attachment to self ends segmental birth-and-death. [Attachment to dharmas] Also called the dharma-self: falsely clinging to the dharma of the Way as real, thinking that there is a dharma to be attained, a Way to be cultivated, birth-and-death to be ended, and nirvāṇa to be realized, and clinging to cultivating the cause and realizing the fruit. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
"The people of the Two Vehicles
(pratyekabuddhas and arhats)
, though they have broken the attachment to person,
still have the attachment to dharmas."

One who severs the attachment to dharmas ends transformation birth-and-death. [Segmental birth-and-death] For beings within the three realms and the six destinies, because of the good and evil karma they have created, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have sections; hence their birth-and-death is called "segmental birth-and-death." One who ends segmental birth-and-death escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Transformation birth-and-death] The sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and have ended segmental birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the Way, deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually grows; this migration from delusion to awakening differs in every period. The passage from an earlier period into a later one is just like a single birth-and-death, and so it is called "transformation birth-and-death." One who ends transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
[Kalpas as dust and sand] Kalpas as numerous as dust and sand — a figure for an extremely long and distant span of time.
Awakened at once and done — this is Tathagata Chan, / in which the six perfections and ten thousand practices are perfected in the essence
In the dream the six destinies are plainly there; / once awakened, the great thousand worlds are empty and bare.

Awakened at once and done: the Tathagata Chan, in which the six perfections and ten thousand practices are all perfected within the true reality of all dharmas. In the dream of ignorance the six paths of rebirth are plainly there; when the dream of ignorance is awakened from, all is limpid and quiescent, and the great thousand worlds simply do not exist.

[Tathagata Chan] "Tathagata Chan" here means the Tathagata Chan spoken of in the Lankavatara Sutra, not the "Tathagata Chan" that is usually set in contrast to "patriarch Chan." The Lankavatara Sutra says:

"What is Tathagata Chan? It means entering the Tathagata's ground, practicing the three blissful abidings marked by the wisdom of self-realized sagehood, and accomplishing the inconceivable work of saving all living beings: this is called Tathagata Chan."
Master Guifeng says:

"If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one's own mind is from the first pure and free of affliction, and that the wisdom-nature beyond outflows is from the first complete, then this mind is the Buddha and in the end is no different. To cultivate in accordance with this is the supreme vehicle of Chan; it is also called the Tathagata's pure Chan, also called the one-practice samādhi, also called the samādhi of true suchness. This is the root of all samādhis; if one cultivates it thought after thought, one will naturally and gradually attain hundreds and thousands of samādhis. Damo
(Bodhidharma)
's disciples, transmitting it from one to another, handed down this very Chan."

(Preface to the Source of Chan.) From this we know: to enter the Tathagata's ground, to practice the three blissful abidings marked by the wisdom of self-realized sagehood, and to accomplish the inconceivable work of saving all living beings — this is called Tathagata Chan. This is the utmost mind-dharma, and what was handed down from one to another among the disciples of Patriarch Bodhidharma is precisely this Chan.

[The marks of the wisdom of self-realized sagehood] The marks of one's own realization of sage-wisdom. [Sage wisdom] The Tathagata's wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma-realm, that is, the wisdom that knows that "all dharmas are from the first unborn"; it is also called the wisdom of the pure dharma-realm. The Lankavatara Sutra says:

"As for the ultimate mark of the wisdom of self-realized sagehood: one does not cling to any mark of dharma, one attains the body of the samādhi of illusion, and one advances and is born in the ground of all Buddhas."
[Marks of practice] The marks of one's practice.

[The "Tathagata Chan" spoken of in contrast to "patriarch Chan"] This was first put forward in the Song of Enlightenment and by Chan Master Yangshan after Master Guifeng (Yangshan was a grand-disciple of Chan Master Baizhang — Guishan awakened upon consulting Baizhang, and Yangshan awakened upon consulting Baizhang). The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp
in the chapter on Yangshan Huiji, says:
"The Master
(Yangshan)
said: You have only attained Tathagata Chan; you have not attained patriarch Chan."
Here patriarch Chan is taken as the mind-seal transmitted by Bodhidharma, and Tathagata Chan as a name for what is not yet complete (see
Xiangyan Strikes the Bamboo

). Afterwards a certain view circulated: that Chan practice is divided according to three grades of faculties — the Chan of the upper and middle faculties is called patriarch Chan, that is, the mind-seal transmitted by Bodhidharma; the Chan of the lower faculties is called Tathagata Chan, such as the Chan of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis. [The four dhyānas and eight samādhis] The four dhyānas are the four meditative concentrations of the form realm; the eight samādhis are the four dhyānas of the form realm together with the four formless concentrations of the formless realm.

[The six perfections and ten thousand practices] In brief, the six perfections; at length, the ten thousand practices. The six perfections include all the gates of practice cultivated by bodhisattvas. [The six perfections] Also called the six pāramitās. "Pāramitā" is a transliteration from Sanskrit; in Chinese it is rendered as du, meaning "to cross over." To cross over means to ferry across the sea of birth-and-death, and "to reach the other shore" means to reach the shore of nirvāṇa. There are six practices of pāramitā (called the six perfections): 1. giving; 2. observing precepts; 3. patience; 4. diligence; 5. meditation; 6. wisdom. [The six perfections and ten thousand practices are perfected within the essence] "Essence" here means the essence of all dharmas, that is, the true reality of all dharmas. One who realizes the true reality of all dharmas is naturally complete in the six perfections and ten thousand practices: realizing the true reality of all dharmas, one relinquishes all conditions — this is the perfection of giving; being originally pure — this is the perfection of precepts; not rejoicing at praise nor growing angry at slander — this is the perfection of patience; having no falsity in thought after thought — this is the perfection of diligence; being inwardly still and unmoved — this is the perfection of meditation; shining with wisdom like the sun — this is the perfection of prajñā. Having reached this ground, the three thousand deportments and eighty thousand fine practices are in accord with the Dharma at every step; not one principle is unperfected, not one matter is incomplete. Hence it is said: "The six perfections and ten thousand practices are perfected within the essence." [In accord with the Dharma] According with the teaching spoken by the Buddha.

[The great thousand worlds] Also called the three-thousand great thousand-world system, it is the region taught and transformed by one Buddha. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world. A thousand small worlds gathered together are called a "small chiliocosm"; a thousand small chiliocosms gathered together are called a "medium chiliocosm"; a thousand medium chiliocosms gathered together are called a "great chiliocosm." Because the thousand is counted three times, a great chiliocosm is also called the "three-thousand great thousand-world system." [In the dream the six destinies are plainly there; once awakened, the great thousand worlds are empty and bare] This is the awakening from the dream of ignorance, the state of "awakened at once and done: the Tathagata Chan."
No merit and no offense, no loss and no gain; / within the nature of quiescent extinction, seeking is in vain
The dusty mirror of old was never polished through; / today it must be laid out clear before you.

No offense and no merit, no loss and no gain: within the nature of quiescent extinction (the true reality of all dharmas) do not ask or seek. The dusty mirror has never been polished until now (a metaphor for the self-nature, which, like a bright mirror, is covered by the rust and grime of greed, hatred, and delusion); today it must be clearly analyzed for you.

[No offense and no merit, no loss and no gain; within the nature of quiescent extinction do not ask or seek] This means: within the true reality of all dharmas there is fundamentally no offense or merit, no loss or gain, and so one should not ask or seek. [Of old] Until now; all along. [Today it must be clearly analyzed] This is Master Shenhui's compassion for students who turn their backs on awakening and join with dust, chasing after offense and merit, loss and gain without cease, and so drift along with karma and forget to return; therefore today he analyzes it clearly for them.
Who is without thought? Who is without birth? / If truly there is no birth and nothing is not born, / then call the mechanical wooden man and ask him
"Seeking the Buddha and applying effort, when shall one succeed?"

Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If there really were no birth and nothing not born, then one would be a mechanical wooden man without thought. How could a mechanical wooden man use the mind to become a Buddha? One would have to seek the Buddha and apply effort. But that is seeking the Dharma outside the mind — could one ever reach the other shore of nirvāṇa that way?

[Mechanical wooden man] A wooden figure made to move by machinery. [If truly there is no birth and nothing is not born, then call the mechanical wooden man and ask him] A mechanical wooden man has no activity of thought — this is no-birth; yet it can move — this is nothing-not-born. "If truly there is no birth and nothing is not born, then call the mechanical wooden man and ask him" means: if there is no activity of thought and yet one can move, would one not become a mechanical wooden man? Chan Master Baozhi says:
"When a mechanical wooden man cultivates the Way, when will it ever reach the other shore?"
(The Record of Pointing at the Moon.) [Using the mind to become a Buddha] The Sixth Patriarch says:
"Simply use this mind and directly realize Buddhahood."

(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.) This is the core of the Sixth Patriarch's sudden teaching. [Sooner or later] Either early or late; it means that the situation will come about one day. [Call the mechanical wooden man and ask him: seeking the Buddha and applying effort, when shall one succeed?] Call the mechanical wooden man (one who knows only the great death) and ask him: by seeking the Buddha and applying effort, will one finally reach the other shore of nirvāṇa?

This passage means that one should pass from the great death (cutting off thought and deliberation) into the great life (letting the mind be free and at ease) — that is, from the work of guarding into the work of letting be. If one always cuts off thought and deliberation, then one is a mechanical wooden man, able to move but without thought. How then could one transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms and perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood? One would have to seek the Buddha and apply effort to accomplish it! But that is seeking the Dharma outside the mind — can one become a Buddha that way?

[Transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms] Transforming the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, mano-consciousness, and ālaya-consciousness) into the four wisdoms (the wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality in nature, and the great perfect mirror wisdom). (For details, see
Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

This passage criticizes those who cling to cutting off thought and deliberation (who can only die the great death and cannot live the great life) and take this to be the ultimate. It is also what the Sixth Patriarch rebukes in the Platform Sutra: "
If one merely thinks of nothing at all and cuts off all thoughts, then when a single thought is cut off one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great mistake!"
The Chan forest mocks such people, saying that they "sit in the cave of black ghosts," "sit behind the shadowy mountain," "drown in dead water," and so on.

[The great death and the great life] For one who cultivates the Way, the first stage is the great death (cutting off thought and deliberation) — this is the work of guarding. When the work of guarding is accomplished, one must enter the second stage, the great life (letting the mind be free and at ease) — this is the work of letting be. One must be able to let the mind be free and at ease without being entangled by the objects of dust; as it is said, "to pass through a hundred flowers without a single leaf clinging to the body," attaining the state in which stillness and illumination are non-dual and emptiness and existence are unobstructed, so that even when the five desires are present one uses them freely without losing the self-nature. The Blue Cliff Record says: one must die the great death once and come back to life before it will do. (Original text:
"One must die the great death once and come back to life before it will do."
) The Fourth Patriarch, instructing Farong, said:
Cutting off thought and deliberation
this dharma
you have now attained
you
have already
accomplished the cutting off of thought and deliberation — the work of guarding is complete
, and there is nothing lacking
the same as "lack"
or missing
Simply let your mind be free and at ease
now begin the work of letting be
letting the mind be free and at ease)

, do not practice contemplation, do not still the mind, do not give rise to greed or hatred, do not harbor sorrow or worry; be broad and unobstructed, follow your own will freely. Do not do good deeds, do not do evil deeds. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in whatever the eye meets and whatever conditions arise, all is the wondrous function of the Buddha; joyful and without care, one is therefore called a Buddha.
For details, see
The Fourth Patriarch's Instruction to Farong
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch there is a koan about Wolun cutting off thought:
"A monk cited Chan Master Wolun's verse: 'Wolun has his artful means, / he can cut off a hundred thoughts; / facing objects his mind does not stir, / and bodhi grows from day to day.' The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)
, hearing it, said: 'This verse does not understand the mind-ground; to practice according to it is to add fetters
(one can only die the great death and cannot live the great life)
. So he showed a verse: Huineng has no artful means, / he cuts off no hundred thoughts; / facing objects his mind rises again and again
(arising in accord with conditions, giving rise to the mind without abiding anywhere, a lively and wondrous function)
, how could bodhi grow
(viewed in terms of the true reality of all dharmas)

[Let go the four great elements, do not clutch them; / in the nature of quiescent extinction, drink and peck as they come. / All compounded things are impermanent, all is empty: / this is the Tathagata's great perfect enlightenment.]
Let go of the

physical body and do not cling to it; in the quiescent essence of all dharmas, eat coarse food and wear rough clothes, drinking and pecking as conditions allow. When one realizes that all compounded things are impermanent and all is empty, this is the Tathagata's great perfect enlightenment.

[The four great elements] All material forms in the world are composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and so they are called "great": the great element of earth, of water, of fire, and of wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, and wind has motion. Here the four great elements refer to the human body.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"What is ignorance? Good men, all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another
(for example, taking east for west, or south for north)

, and falsely take the four great elements as the mark of their own bodies and the reflected images of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own minds. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good men, in the sky there are truly no flowers; the diseased person clings to them falsely. Because of this false clinging, he is confused not only about the nature of this empty space but also about where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he revolves in birth-and-death; this is called ignorance."

(Translation: What is ignorance? Good men, all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversions, taking the false as real — this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the physical body formed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own body, and the thoughts arising when the six sense-faculties come into contact with the six sense-objects as the mark of his own mind. It is like an eye affected by illness that falsely sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good men, in reality there are no flowers in the sky; this is an illusion falsely clung to by the diseased eye. Because of this false clinging, one not only falsely holds empty space to be real but also believes that real flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings are inverted and deluded and falsely take the illusory body and mind to be real, clinging to them as "I," they revolve in birth-and-death; this is why it is called ignorance.) [Reflected images of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-faculties come into contact with the six sense-objects; because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the reflected images of the six sense-objects — the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects.

[Let go the four great elements, do not clutch them] Let go of attachment to the body. The reason people cannot live free and unconstrained is mostly that they crave comfort and pleasure for the body, making the mind a slave of the form (the spirit enslaved by the body); this is the typical expression of clinging to the four great elements (the body). [Nature of quiescent extinction] The quiescent essence of all dharmas, that is, the true reality of all dharmas. [Drink and peck (
zhuó
)] To drink water and peck food
a figure for living freely and at ease. The Zhuangzi,
"Nourishing the Lord of Life," says:
"A marsh pheasant pecks once every ten steps and drinks once every hundred, and does not pray
qí
, to pray)
to be kept in a cage
(a pen)

The Subcommentary of Cheng Xuanying says: "Drinking and pecking at ease, free and unfettered and rambling — how would it wish to enter a cage and seek to be fed! This is a figure for one who nourishes life, withdrawing serenely and living in reclusion, finding contentment only in the sounds of the forest — how would he envy glory and splendor!" As the common saying goes:
"The caged chicken has its food, but the soup and the knife are near; the wild crane has no grain, but heaven and earth are wide."
[Marsh pheasant (
zhì
)] A wild pheasant of the marshes. [Forest sounds (
lài
)] The sound made by wind blowing through trees.
[All compounded things are impermanent] All things in the world change without constancy.
The Nirvana Sutra says:
"All compounded things are impermanent — this is the dharma of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss."
(For details, see
Notes on the Snow Mountain Verse

[All compounded things are impermanent, all is empty: this is the Tathagata's great perfect enlightenment] To realize that all compounded things are impermanent and all is empty — this is the Tathagata's great perfect enlightenment. The Diamond Sutra says:
"Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha."
(For the annotation, see
Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
) [One is named a Buddha] That is, one is called a Buddha. Here the word rendered "all" (zhu) functions like the particle zhi, as in "Neng shi zhu hu?" ("Can you serve him?").
The definitive teaching, revealing the true
vehicle
; yet some will not accept and willfully press their questions
To cut straight to the root is what the Buddhas seal; to search the branches and pluck the leaves is what I cannot do.

This is the definitively correct teaching, the true path to Buddhahood, yet there are those who will not accept it and willfully press their questions and objections. To do the work from the root (cutting straight to the root — a figure for the sudden teaching) is what the Buddhas have sealed and approved; to go searching the branches and plucking the leaves (a figure for the gradual teaching) is what I cannot do.

[Definitive teaching] A single word that decides the matter, with no other teaching ever to follow. [True vehicle] The true teaching. "Vehicle" (yana) uses the figures of a boat or raft and a cart to describe the teaching that ferries one across the sea of birth-and-death to the other shore of nirvāṇa. [Will not accept] Does not agree, does not accept. [Press] To pursue to the bottom. [Cutting straight to the root] Cultivation means severing ignorance in order to become a Buddha. Severing ignorance is like felling a poisonous tree: one should cut straight through its root rather than search the branches and pluck the leaves. [To cut straight to the root is what the Buddhas seal; to search the branches and pluck the leaves is what I cannot do] "Cutting straight to the root" refers to the sudden teaching transmitted by the Sixth Patriarch; "searching the branches and plucking the leaves" refers to the gradual teaching transmitted by Shenxiu. [The two teachings of sudden and gradual in Chan] In the south, the lineage of Huineng upheld the sudden teaching, known in the world as "southern suddenness"; in the north, the lineage of Shenxiu upheld the gradual teaching, known as "northern gradualness." [Sudden teaching] The teaching that does not pass through stages and steps but points directly to the source and brings about sudden awakening. [Gradual teaching] The teaching in which one awakens by advancing gradually in sequence.

The division between the Southern and Northern sudden and gradual teachings began with Master Shenhui's attack on the Chan teaching of Shenxiu's line: "The lineage is collateral, the Dharma-gate is gradual" (Chart of the Transmission of the Mind-Ground of the Chan Gate in China). Afterwards there arose an even tenser struggle over the Dharma-lineage: "The followers of sudden and gradual look on one another as enemies; the Southern and Northern schools oppose each other like Chu and Han" (General Preface to the Collected Interpretations of the Sources of Chan). Judging from the shifting fortunes of the two lines, in the
th century's second half and the
th century's first half, the Chan style of Shenxiu's line all but shrouded northern China, and its power and influence far surpassed those of Huineng's line. It was only in the
th century's middle years, and especially after the Huichang persecution of Buddhism in the middle of the
th century, that it gradually declined; by the end of the
th century it verged on extinction. Huineng's line, by the

th century, developed rapidly in the south. Mazu Daoyi, Qingyuan Xingsi, and above all the "five houses" such as Linji and Caodong pushed Huineng's Chan to a new stage and more vividly championed the Chan style of the sudden-enlightenment Dharma-gate. The two branches of Mazu Daoyi and Qingyuan Xingsi, as the chief representatives of Huineng's line, later increasingly became the mainstream of Chinese Chan.
The mani pearl that man does not know is gathered and kept within the Tathagata-garbha.
Six divine functions, empty yet not empty; a single orb of perfect light, colored yet not colored.

The wish-fulfilling jewel, which people do not know, is within the Tathagata-garbha. Once this mani pearl is found, the six faculties become liberated (the six divine functions). This six-fold divine function of the six faculties being liberated is empty and yet not empty; the orb of light of the mani pearl is colored and yet not colored.

Mani pearl (mo ni zhu): the wish-fulfilling jewel; here it is a metaphor for the wondrous function that appears after one realizes the Tathagata-garbha. Tathagata-garbha (ru lai zang): the original nature. As for the Tathagata-garbha,
see in detail
Mind, Self-nature, and Tathagata-garbha
Six divine functions (liu ban shen yong): the wondrous function in which the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) become liberated. The Surangama Sutra says:
“When one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties become liberated.”

Six divine functions, empty and not empty (liu ban shen yong kong, bu kong): the six divine functions, viewed from principle, are empty; viewed from phenomena, they are not empty. One orb of perfect light, colored yet not colored (yi ke yuan guang se fei se): the orb of light of the mani pearl, viewed from principle, is not colored; viewed from phenomena, it is colored.
Purify the five eyes and attain the five powers; only through personal realization can one know, hard to fathom!
To see forms in a mirror is not hard; to seize the moon in water, how could one grasp it?

The state of purifying the five eyes and attaining the five powers can only be known through one’s own personal realization (not through speculation). People regard the cultivation of a realized one as if looking at forms in a mirror: to imitate him on the surface is not difficult, but it is like grasping the moon in water — one cannot obtain the moon. Only by doing the practice from the very root oneself, and personally realizing it, is one on the right path.

Purify the five eyes (jing wu yan): the flesh eye is not deluded by objects; the divine eye sees through to all things; the wisdom eye’s insight is clear and penetrating; the Dharma eye sees that nature is originally empty; the Buddha eye regards things and self with equality.

Attain the five powers (de wu li): once the five eyes are purified, the five powers naturally manifest before one. The five powers (wu li): the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith can destroy all evil beliefs; the power of vigor can destroy the laziness of the body; the power of mindfulness can destroy all evil thoughts; the power of concentration can destroy all confused imaginings; and the power of wisdom can destroy all the delusions of the three realms. Only through personal realization can one know, hard to fathom (wei zheng nai zhi nan ke ce): the gate of the ground of mind can only be known through realization, and cannot be measured by the feelings of ordinary beings. To see forms in a mirror is not hard, to seize the moon in water how could one grasp it (jing li kan xing jian bu nan, shui zhong zhuo yue zen nian de): it is said that whenever Einstein gave a lecture, his chauffeur sat in the back row, listening intently and taking notes. One day the chauffeur said to Einstein: “I too could give your lecture.” Einstein said: “Very well, next time you deliver it for me.” So, with Einstein’s consent, the chauffeur joyfully gave a fluent lecture. Just as he was triumphantly concluding, the audience began to ask questions, and the chauffeur was dumbfounded. There is a similar matter in the Chan school: when Master Dahui went to Fujian to guide Chan practitioners, he found that each and every one of them spoke remarkably, and he was greatly astonished. Upon questioning, they admitted: “We have memorized these from the Blue Cliff Record; we have not, in fact, awakened.” (This is treating the old masters’ cases as ready-made replies, taking clever advantage, and applying them solely to deal with the examinations of a student’s studied practice.) Panshan says:
“The one road on high, the thousand sages do not transmit; the student wears out his body, as a monkey grasping for its shadow.”
(From the Transmission of the Lamp)
Constantly walking alone, constantly solitary in step, the attained ones roam together the road of nirvana.
His tune is ancient, his spirit pure, his manner of itself is lofty; his face gaunt, his bones firm, yet men do not regard him.

He constantly walks alone, constantly solitary in step, roaming together with the awakened upon the road that leads to nirvana. His bearing is lofty and antique, his mind clear and serene, and his manner in the Way is naturally noble. Yet his countenance is worn and his bones are firm, and worldly people pay him no heed.
Roam (you): to walk calmly and at ease.
The poor son of the Buddha, in word calls himself poor; in truth his body is poor, his Way is not poor.
Being poor, his body is ever clad in tattered wool; possessing the Way, his heart conceals the priceless jewel.

The poor son of the Buddha, in word calls himself a poor monk; in truth his body is poor and his Way is rich. His body being poor, he is ever clad in ragged clothes; his Way being rich, his heart stores the priceless jewel.
Son of the Buddha (shi zi): a disciple of Sakyamuni Buddha; this is the general term for members of the sangha. Lu he (
lu he
): torn, ragged clothes.
The priceless jewel, its use is never exhausted; benefiting things and responding to occasions, it never hoards.
In the body, the three bodies and the four wisdoms are perfectly complete; in the ground of mind, the eight liberations and the six superknowledges are stamped.

The priceless jewel, its use without end; it benefits all things and, responding to occasions, is given without the least stinginess. In the body the three bodies and the four wisdoms are complete; in the ground of mind the eight liberations and the six superknowledges are stamped.

The eight liberations (ba jie): namely the eight samadhi-releases: first, having thoughts of form, one contemplates the objects of form — this is the liberation. Second, with no thought of form inwardly, one contemplates outer forms — this is the liberation. Third, the pure liberation where one attains bodily witness and dwells in its completeness — this is the liberation. Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space. Fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothing whatsoever. Seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, where one attains bodily witness and dwells in its completeness. The three bodies (san shen): the Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the response-body. The Dharma-body, also called the self-nature body, or the Dharma-nature body, is originally possessed by everyone; only we sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The reward-body is formed of the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, and is distinguished as the reward-body of self-enjoyment and the reward-body of other-enjoyment: the reward-body of self-enjoyment is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the joy of the Dharma realized within; the reward-body of other-enjoyment is the body manifested by the Buddha to speak the Dharma to the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The response-body, also called the accommodating transformation body, or the metamorphic body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the opportunities and conditions of sentient beings. The four wisdoms (si zhi): the wisdom of accomplished action, the wisdom of wondrous contemplation, the wisdom of equality, and the great mirror wisdom. The wisdom of accomplished action is accomplished by transforming the five fallen-and-defiled consciousnesses (the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that accomplishes all deeds benefiting all sentient beings. The wisdom of wondrous contemplation is accomplished by transforming the sixth fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the mind-consciousness), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that observes all dharmas and the capacities of all sentient beings, and gives the medicine according to the illness and transforms the ordinary into the sage. The wisdom of equality is accomplished by transforming the seventh fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the manas), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that penetrates the principle of selflessness and equality, and on that account raises the great compassion without conditions toward all sentient beings. The great mirror wisdom is accomplished by transforming the eighth fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the alaya), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that contemplates all phenomena and principles without anything not understood; this wisdom, pure and clear, sees through to both inner and outer, like a great round mirror, illuminating all things.
The superior man, once resolved, is done with all; the middling and the lower, though much learned, do not believe.
But when one alone unbinds the soiled garment from within his own breast, who can boast of vigor toward the outside?

The superior man realizes the true reality of all dharmas (once resolved), and being once resolved, is done with all; but many of the middling and lower sort, on hearing it, do not believe. One can only personally cut off ignorance and realize the original nature — how then can it be proclaimed outwards to others?
Once resolved (yi jue): this is the “realizing the true reality” spoken of earlier. Done with all (yi qie le): the earlier song says:
“Realize the true reality, and there is neither person nor dharma.”

Because one has realized the true reality of all dharmas, both the attachment to person and the attachment to dharma are cut off, and of course all is done. Therefore this is an extremely perfect and sudden gate, cutting straight to the very root. Unbinding the soiled garment (jie gou yi): cutting off ignorance and realizing the original nature (the Tathagata-garbha).
The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The Tathagata-garbha is pure in its own nature, and turns the thirty-two marks to enter into the bodies of all sentient beings. Like a great precious gem wrapped in a soiled garment.”
Let him slander, let him condemn; to set fire to the sky only wearies oneself in vain.
When I hear it, it is like drinking sweet dew; melting away, I suddenly enter the inconceivable.
Even if the iron wheel whirled above my head, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom is never lost.

People not only do not believe in this perfect and sudden gate, but on the contrary revile and slander it. If one pays them no heed (let him slander, let him condemn), these revilings and slanders are like raising fire to burn the sky — they burn nothing, and dying away of themselves, merely waste effort. When I hear these revilings and slanders, it is like drinking the sweet dew; after melting away the self-nature, I suddenly enter the inconceivable state. Even if the iron wheel whirled above my head, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom is never for a moment lost.

Let him slander, let him condemn (cong ta bang, ren ta fei): allow him to revile, allow him to oppose. Master Shenhui, the author of the Song of the Realization of the Way, in order to spread the Sixth Patriarch’s sudden teaching, endured slander, defamation, and persecution.
According to the record:

Shenhui, fond of study from a young age, heard that the great master of Caoxi in Lingnan was greatly exalting the Way of Chan, and so, emulating Sudhana’s fifty-three pilgrimages, he traveled from afar, not shunning a thousand li, to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch; his feet were torn and he had no shoes, so he tore his clothes to wrap his feet and went on. After seeing the patriarch, he attended upon him constantly and received the sudden teaching in full. The Sixth Patriarch praised him, saying:
“Little Master Shenhui, you have attained that good and not-good are equal, that praise and blame move you not, that sorrow and joy are not born.”
(From the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
the tenth chapter, the Chapter of Entrustment)

Although Huineng, having received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, became the Sixth Patriarch, his sudden teaching spread only within the Lingnan region alone. In all the vast land of China, it was almost entirely the world of Shenxiu’s gradual teaching. After Shenxiu passed away, his great disciple Puji continued to propagate his lineage, flourishing for a time, and the people of the day called him “the master of the Dharma in the two capitals, the teacher of the three emperors” (the two capitals referring to the western capital Chang’an and the eastern capital Luoyang, and the three emperors to Empress Wu Zetian, Emperor Zhongzong, and Emperor Ruizong). Puji also regarded Shenxiu as the orthodox heir of Bodhidharma’s school, and established him as the Sixth Patriarch, while calling himself the Seventh Patriarch.

In order to protect the right Dharma, Shenhui entered the capital city of Luoyang, and, heedless of the threat to his very life, made the lion’s roar, greatly propagating the Chan Dharma of Caoxi. He established an open, unhindered assembly at the Dayun Monastery in Huatai, Henan, and openly engaged in debate with Master Chongyuan, then renowned in both capitals and known even beyond the sea, concerning the right and wrong, the true and the false, of the southern and northern schools of Chan. He attacked the northern school for “borrowed transmission and gradual practice,” and wrote the Record of Illuminating the Essential Doctrine, determining the southern Huineng as the sudden school (definitively establishing the southern Huineng as the sudden school) and the northern Shenxiu as the gradual teaching (the northern Shenxiu as the gradual teaching). Establishing the essential purport of the southern school, he caused the sudden teaching to be greatly spread in Luoyang and to circulate throughout the empire, a bright lamp shining high, generation after generation transformed by it.

Heedless of the threat to his very life, making the lion’s roar (bu gu xing ming wei xie zuo shi zi hou): according to the record in the Treatise Determining Right and Wrong in the Southern School, at the time Chongyuan threatened Shenhui, saying: “Master Puji’s name covers the whole land, known throughout the world, proclaimed by every mouth, and beyond thought. To criticize him in this way, is this not to make an enemy of your own body and life?” Shenhui answered: “Master Puji’s school differs from the southern school; I myself weigh the right and wrong and determine its essential purport. I now say that to spread the Mahayana and establish the right Dharma, causing all sentient beings to know and hear it — how could I begrudge my body and life?” Chongyuan again asked: “In doing this, is it not to seek fame and profit?” Shenhui answered: “I do not spare even my life; how could I be concerned with fame and profit?” This fully shows Shenhui’s spirit of forgetting his body for the sake of the Dharma. For this reason, Shenhui suffered the jealousy and wrongs of the northern school to the utmost; the censor Lü Yi, currying favor with Puji, falsely accused Shenhui of gathering disciples, suspecting him of fomenting trouble. According to the Great Commentary on the Surangama Sutra, Shenhui, within less than two years, was forced to move his dwelling four times: “In the twelfth year of the Tianbao era, being slandered as gathering a crowd, an edict banished him to Yiyang Commandery, and then moved him to Wudang Commandery. By the thirteenth year, by imperial grace, he was moved to Xiangzhou. By the seventh month, another edict moved him to Kaiyuan Monastery in Jingzhou. All of this was the destruction carried out by members of the northern school.” In the third year of Shenhui’s banishment, the situation suddenly changed, and the rebellion of An and Shi broke out; Lü Yi was killed by the rebels, and only then did the persecution cease. The unhindered assembly (wu zhe hui): this kind of assembly makes offerings indiscriminately to all, as people today hold a thousand-monk feast to form bonds with ten thousand persons; anyone may take part, without any bar or restriction.
Regarding evil words as merit, this becomes to me a good teacher.
If enmity and kinship did not arise through mockery and slander, how could one show the compassionate endurance-power of the unborn?

To regard (to view) evil words as merit: this is the good teacher who perfects me. If it were not that enmity and kinship arise on account of reviling and slander, how could I manifest the compassionate endurance-power of the unborn (the realization that all dharmas are wholly empty and still), in which enmity and kinship are equal?
Mockery and slander (shan
shan
bang): mocking (to ridicule and sneer) and defamation.

blocks.text: Five: Through in Both the Essential and the Expounded

inline.s: Through in the essential and through in the expounded, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom does not dwell in emptiness.
Not only have I now alone thoroughly arrived; the bodies of all the Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges are also the same.

I am through in both the essential and the expounded, with the perfect light of concentration and wisdom, not dwelling in emptiness. Not only have I now alone thoroughly arrived; the Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges have also realized the essence in this way.

Through in both the essential and the expounded (zong shuo ju tong): one who penetrates the profound essential purport in the Chan school is called through in the essential; one who can face the assembly and freely preach the teaching to transform beings is called through in the expounded. One who is through in both the essential and the expounded is a great master. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The Buddha told Mahamati: All sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two aspects of penetration, called the essential penetration and the expounded penetration.”
The commentary says: “The essential is the root of the Way; the expounded is the trace of the teaching.”
The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching; the hundred beasts, hearing it, all split with terror.
The fragrant elephant in flight loses his majesty; the dragons and devas listen in stillness and are filled with joy.

The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching; the hundred beasts are terrified out of their wits (their gall is burst). The fragrant elephant, in flight, loses his majesty; the dragons and devas, listening in stillness, are filled with joy.

The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching (shi zi hou, wu wei shuo): see the annotation “heedless of the threat to his very life, making the lion’s roar” above. The hundred beasts (bai shou): these refer to the disciples and followers of Master Puji. These men held great power in the western capital Chang’an and the eastern capital Luoyang, reaching from the imperial court on high down to the government offices, gentry, and officials below. The fragrant elephant (xiang xiang): the mighty and robust elephant, from the bones at its ear-gate secretes a liquid of fragrant scent, being much mightier and more robust than the ordinary elephant. Here it refers to Master Puji, “the master of the Dharma in the two capitals, the teacher of the three emperors.” The dragons and devas (tian long): the devas and dragons; here they refer to the bodhisattvas who have greatly opened up the perfect understanding.
Wandering the rivers and seas, crossing the mountains and streams, seeking a teacher and visiting the Way for the sake of Chan.
Ever since I recognized the road of Caoxi, I know that birth and death are no longer my concern.

Wandering the rivers and seas, crossing the mountains and streams, seeking a teacher and visiting the Way for the sake of Chan. Ever since I recognized the road of Caoxi (the Sixth Patriarch’s sudden teaching), I know that birth and death are no longer my concern (only then did I know that birth and death are but an illusion).
Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; in speaking, in silence, in motion and stillness, the body is at ease.
Even meeting the sharp blade, one is ever serene; even were poison brought, it, too, is a thing of no account.
My teacher, having met Dipamkara Buddha, for many aeons was the ascetic of patient endurance.]

Walking too is in Chan, sitting too is in Chan; whether speaking (words) or silent (no words), whether moving or still, all is serene and at ease. Even if the sharp blade is laid upon me, I am likewise calm; even if poison schemes against me, it is a thing of no account. The reason my teacher (Sakyamuni Buddha) met Dipamkara Buddha is that for many aeons he had been the ascetic of patient endurance.

This is the true portrayal of Master Shenhui’s mind and conduct amid exile and persecution. In former days, Master Hanshan, having met with trouble on account of spreading the Dharma, was cast into the imperial dungeon; when life and death were yet undecided, he did not diminish even one thought of joy — this too is the same state. Master Hanshan wrote: “In recent days, because I spread the Dharma I fell into persecution, and the emperor was greatly enraged (the master, being slandered for spreading the Dharma, enraged the sovereign, was arrested and cast into prison, tortured with severe punishment, with life and death undecided), like a bolt from a clear sky, at which hearers stopped their ears. From my arrest until the exile from the capital, for more than two hundred days I experienced every hardship, beyond all words. From first to last, I beheld the one thought of joy within me, and it was not in the least diminished from usual; those who saw it were all greatly astonished. As for the sudden calamity of life and death, by it others were alarmed on my account; but when they saw my joy undiminished from its usual state, they were the more astonished. I am not astonished at the calamity of life and death at which men are astonished, while men are astonished that I am not astonished — perhaps there is some principle in it!” (The original is found in the Collected Works from the Dream Wanderings
in “Shown to the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang”)

Serene (tan tan): perfectly calm. Even were (jia rao): even if, granting that. Of no account (xian xian): trifling, as a casual thing. The ascetic of patient endurance (ren ru xian): Sakyamuni Buddha, in his causal stage, was the ascetic of patient endurance, cultivating the practice of patience. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha says:

“Subhuti! Further, reflect on the past, when for five hundred lives I was the ascetic of patient endurance. In those lives I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, and no mark of a life.”
This chapter says:
“My teacher
(Sakyamuni Buddha)
, having met Dipamkara Buddha, for many aeons was the ascetic of patient endurance.”
From this it can be seen that the practice of patient endurance is the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.
How many times born, how many times dead; drifting through birth and death, with no certain rest.
Ever since suddenly awakening to the unborn, what sorrow or joy is there in honor and disgrace?

Master Shenhui had passed through birth and death many times; whether to live or to die, his future was undecided (hard to foresee). But ever since he suddenly awakened to the unborn Dharma, what is there to sorrow or to rejoice in honor, disgrace, birth, and death?
Entering the deep mountains, dwelling in the aranya, beneath the steep, secluded, and ancient pines
at ease in silent sitting in the wild monk’s home; dwelling in profound quiet, truly free and easy.
Entering the deep mountains and dwelling in the aranya, beneath the steep and distant old pines, is the home of the wild monk who sits at ease; to dwell here in quiet peace is truly free and easy.
This paragraph describes the situation of dwelling in the mountains after one has attained the purport.
Aranya (lan ruo): the abbreviation of aranya, a place where monks practice in quietness. Cen yin (
cen yin
): the steep, lofty appearance of the mountains. You sui (
sui
): a remote, distant place. Qu (
qu
ji): quiet and still.

blocks.text: Six: When One Awakens, It Is Done

inline.s: When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied; it is unlike all conditioned dharmas.
Clinging
to marks, giving brings the blessing of heavenly rebirth, like shooting an arrow upward at the empty sky.

When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied (this is the unconditioned Dharma), and is unlike all conditioned dharmas. Giving while clinging to marks (a conditioned Dharma) at most attains the blessing of heavenly rebirth; this is like raising one’s head and shooting an arrow at the empty sky.

When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied (jue ji le, bu shi gong): having awakened to the true reality of all dharmas, then all is done, and there is no further need to apply effort to any practice; it is the effortless practice. Effortless practice (wu gong yong xing): to practice without borrowing the three of body, speech, and mind, moving freely and spontaneously in a natural state. Conditioned dharmas (you wei fa): ordinarily, conditioned dharmas refer to all things produced by the union of conditions. Here conditioned dharmas are spoken of in regard to cultivation. Cultivation is divided into conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas: to practice while clinging to marks is a conditioned Dharma; to practice while free from marks is an unconditioned Dharma. For example, if the mind abides in dharmas (clinging to marks) and practices giving, this is a conditioned Dharma; if the mind does not abide in dharmas (free from marks) and practices giving, this is an unconditioned Dharma. The Diamond Sutra says:
“If a bodhisattva’s mind abides in dharmas
(clinging to marks)
and he practices giving, it is like a man entering darkness
(the same as “darkness”)
, and he sees nothing. If a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in dharmas
(free from marks)
and he practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, whose sight the light of the sun illumines, and he sees all manner of forms.”
It also says:
“All the sages and holy ones differ only by virtue of the unconditioned Dharma.”
(See in detail
The Diamond Sutra Explained
In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections spoken by the Buddha, it is said:

“The Buddha said: A renunciant who has left home cuts off desire and abandons love, recognizes the source of his own mind, reaches the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned Dharma. Inwardly he has nothing attained; outwardly he seeks nothing; his mind is not bound to the Way
(not clinging to the Way)
, nor does it create karma
(nor does it generate karma)
; with no thought and no doing, neither practicing nor realizing
(practicing without practice, realizing without realization)
Without passing through the stages
(without passing through the fifty-two stages)
, yet of himself he is supremely honored; this is called the Way.”
(See in detail
Annotation to the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections

The fifty-two stages (wu shi er ge jie wei): a bodhisattva’s practice has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, the stage of equal enlightenment, and the stage of wondrous enlightenment; the stage of wondrous enlightenment is Buddhahood.

Clinging to marks (zhuo xiang): to take marks as real, and so to love and hate, to take and reject. Giving while clinging to marks (zhuo xiang bu shi): if, in giving, one realizes the three wheels as empty, this is mark-free giving, also called formless giving; if one does not, it is giving while clinging to marks, also called marked giving. The three wheels as empty (san lun ti kong): the giver, the receiver, and the thing given are called the three wheels. After giving, these three wheels’ marks are not retained in the mind; this is called “the three wheels as empty.”
Mark-free giving is endowed with the six perfections (the six paramitas). In the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra
chapter one, the Introductory Chapter, the Buddha says:
“Sariputra! When a bodhisattva-mahasattva practices the perfection of giving in the prajna paramita
(that is, mark-free giving)
, by virtue of the power of his skillful wisdom he can be complete with the perfection of dana
(giving)
, the perfection of sila
(precept-keeping)
, the perfection of ksanti
(patience)
, the perfection of virya
(vigor)
, the perfection of dhyana
(meditation)
, and the perfection of prajna
(wisdom)

. Sariputra said to the Buddha: World-honored One, how is it that when a bodhisattva-mahasattva practices giving, by virtue of the power of his skillful wisdom he is complete with the perfection of dana and so on to the perfection of prajna? The Buddha told Sariputra: Because the giver, the receiver, and the goods are unobtainable
(the three wheels as empty)
, he is complete with the perfection of dana. Because the sinful and the sinless are unobtainable, he is complete with the perfection of sila. Because the mind is unmoved, he is complete with the
chan

perfection of ksanti. Because body and mind are vigorous and never slack, he is complete with the perfection of virya. Because he is neither scattered nor dull, he is complete with the perfection of dhyana. Because he knows all dharmas as unobtainable, he is complete with the perfection of prajna.”
In the Great Prajna Paramita Sutra
chapter two, the Chapter on Studying and Contemplating, the Buddha says:

“The bodhisattvas-mahasattvas who cultivate the prajna paramita can thus for real know: if a bodhisattva-mahasattva, taking non-acquisition as his skillful means, cultivates the perfection of giving, and penetratively understands that all givers, all receivers, and all things given are unobtainable
(the three wheels as empty)
, then this giving, as a skillful and adroit means, can fulfill the perfections of giving, pure precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna.”

The six perfections (liu du): also called the six paramitas, the six practices by which one can cross from this shore of the suffering of birth and death to the other shore of the bliss of nirvana; namely, giving, precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna. Giving ferries over stinginess and greed; precept-keeping ferries over transgression; patience ferries over anger; vigor ferries over sloth; meditation ferries over distraction; and prajna ferries over ignorance.

Giving while clinging to marks brings the blessing of heavenly rebirth (zhuo xiang bu shi sheng tian fu): giving while clinging to marks at most attains the blessing of heavenly rebirth and cannot escape the wheel of the six realms. The Pointing at the Moon Record says:
“Emperor Wu of Liang asked Bodhidharma
(Master Bodhidharma)
: ‘I have built monasteries and ordained monks without number — what merit is there in this?’
(What sort of merit is there? — Emperor Wu thought his merit was exceedingly great; he was clinging to marks.)
Bodhidharma said: ‘No merit.’ The emperor said: ‘Why is there no merit?’ Bodhidharma said: ‘This is but the small fruit of humans and devas
(this is merely the small retribution of being reborn as a human or a deva)
, a cause that is defiled. Like a shadow following the form, though it has being yet it is not real.”
Defiled (you lou):

lou is another name for afflictions; the matter that contains afflictions (greed, anger, and ignorance) is called defiled; the matter free of afflictions is called undefiled. Merit (gong de): cultivation is the merit (gong); the purity of body and mind is the virtue (de); extinguishing the ignorance within the mind is the merit (gong); the manifestation of wisdom is the virtue (de). Blessedness (fu de): the portion of blessing gained by cultivating the wholesome acts of humans and devas. Blessedness and merit differ: the externally cultivated defiled good of worldly deeds is “blessedness,” while the inwardly realized undefiled wisdom of the Buddha-nature is “merit.” Moreover, in the cultivation of the Way, if one practices while clinging to marks, that is “blessedness”; if one practices while free from marks, that alone is “merit.”
When the force is spent, the arrow falls back down, summoning an unhappy next life.
How does it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true reality, which in one leap enters directly the ground of the Tathagata?

Once the arrow’s force is spent, it falls back down (this is a metaphor for the fact that once the blessings of heaven are exhausted one falls into the other five realms), summoning an unhappy next life. How does it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true reality, which, without passing through the stages, directly realizes Buddhahood?

How does it compare (zheng si): how can it be like. Summoning an unhappy next life (zhao de lai sheng bu ru yi): for if once the blessed retribution is exhausted, the next life is miserable. Hanshan says:

“I have seen the wheel-turning king, a thousand sons ever around him; by the ten wholesome deeds he transforms the four heavens, adorned with many precious things. The seven treasures ever accompany his person, adorned most wondrously and well. But once the blessed retribution is spent, it is like a
qi
bird among the reeds
(like a bird lodging in the reed thicket)
.— He will even become a worm upon the ox’s neck
(he will become an insect on the ox’s neck)
, receiving the karma-paths of the six destinies.”

(From the Collected Poems of the Master of Cold Mountain.) In one leap entering directly the ground of the Tathagata (yi chao zhi ru ru lai di): without passing through the stages, directly realizing Buddhahood. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections spoken by the Buddha, it is said:

“The Buddha said: A renunciant who has left home cuts off desire and abandons love, recognizes the source of his own mind, reaches the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned Dharma. Inwardly he has nothing attained; outwardly he seeks nothing; his mind is not bound to the Way
(not clinging to the Way)
, nor does it create karma
(nor does it generate karma)
; with no thought and no doing, neither practicing nor realizing
(practicing without practice, realizing without realization)
Without passing through the stages
(without passing through the fifty-two stages)
, yet of himself he is supremely honored; this is called the Way.”
Once you attain the root, do not worry over the branches; it is like pure lapis lazuli holding the precious moon.
Able to understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting self and others, it is never exhausted.

Once you attain the root (just realize the patient endurance of the unborn Dharma), do not worry over the branches (there is no need to be anxious about the miraculous functions and other branch-and-twig matters); then it is like pure lapis lazuli containing the precious moon (the perfectly bright, exquisite mind). Able to realize this perfectly bright, exquisite mind, the wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting self and others will never be exhausted.
Like pure lapis lazuli holding the precious moon (ru jing liu li han bao yue): the Surangama Sutra says:

“If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then the faculties present before you interfunction with one another. From this interfunctioning, one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s vajra-like, non-attached wisdom. The perfectly bright, exquisite mind then transforms and reveals within it, like pure lapis lazuli containing within it the precious moon. In this way one surmounts the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the four stages of expedient aid, the ten vajra grounds practiced by the bodhisattva, and the perfect radiance of equal enlightenment, and enters the marvellous and adorned sea of the Tathagata.”

The river moon shines, the pine wind blows; through the long night and the clear evening, what is there to do? The Buddha-nature and the jewel of precepts are stamped in the ground of mind; mist, dew, clouds, and rosy clouds are the garments upon the body.

The bright moon over the river shines upon it, the wind through the pine wood blows; in this long night and clear evening, what is there to do? — The Buddha-nature and the jewel of precepts are stamped in the ground of mind; mist, dew, clouds, and rosy clouds are like the garments upon the body.
This paragraph describes Master Shenhui's situation of pure cultivation while dwelling in the mountains.
Yongye (the long night): the long night. Jie zhu (the pearl of the precepts): the precepts are pure and white, adorning the human body, like a bright pearl. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Earnestly cultivate the pure and quiet precepts, as one guards a bright pearl.”
Wulu yunxia ti shang yi (rain, mist, clouds, and rosy clouds for the garments of the body): this shows that Master Shenhui sat in meditation day and night in the open air.
The dragon-subduing bowl, the tiger-releasing staff, the two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly.
It is not to display a mere form in vain, but the very traces of the Tathagata's jeweled staff.

Carrying the dragon-subduing alms bowl and holding the tiger-releasing staff, with the two-pronged golden rings on the staff ringing brightly and clearly, he wandered freely along the rivers and lakes. It is not that I cling to form and make a show, but that this is the Dharma-code (the rule) handed down in person by the Tathagata.
This paragraph describes Master Shenhui's situation of entering the marketplace to deliver and transform beings.
Xiang long bo (the dragon-subduing bowl): the Buddha's bowl that subdued the venomous dragon. The Collection of the Buddha's Past Deeds
in the chapter “The Three Kasyapa Brothers” says:
“The Tathagata converted
(delivered)

the three Kasyapa brothers, and came to the village of Uruvilva, seeking a place to rest. There was a thatched hut, and a disciple of Kasyapa, sick with dysentery, defiled the hut, and so in anger was expelled
bin

and on dying became a venomous dragon, harming people and beasts in this hut. Kasyapa wished to subdue it, and made offerings to the fire god, but the power of the fire god was not enough. The Tathagata dwelt within the hut and, serene, entered the chamber of meditation. Then the venomous dragon spewed a blaze to menace the Tathagata, and the Tathagata also entered the samadhi of fire-light, his body issuing forth a great fire, and the hut blazed as a great conflagration. When the venomous dragon saw that the place where the Tathagata sat alone was serene and without fire, it went of itself to where the Buddha was, and leaping up entered the Buddha's bowl.”
The Biographies of Eminent Monks
in “Spiritual Marvels,” the lower section,
in “Monk She” says:
“Monk She was a man of the Western Regions

He came to Chang’an in the twelfth year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian, and could by secret incantation summon down the spirit-dragons. Every time there was drought, Jian would ask him to charm the dragon, and presently the dragon would descend into the bowl, and the sky would send a great rain. Jian and his ministers and officials came in person to look into the bowl, and all marveled at the strangeness.”

After this, the “dragon-subduing bowl” became a general term for a monk's alms bowl. Jie hu xi (the tiger-releasing staff): the Chan master Sengchou of the Northern Qi once released the fighting of two tigers with his staff. Xi zhang (the staff): used by renunciates while traveling on foot. The staff has two rings (the two prongs), and each ring has three hoops. The two prongs represent the two truths of the mundane and the supreme, and each prong has three hoops, in all six hoops, representing the six perfections and the myriad practices. Liang gu jin huan ming lili (the two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly): the two-pronged golden rings ring brightly and clearly. Xiang long bo, jie hu xi, liang gu jin huan ming lili (the dragon-subduing bowl, the tiger-releasing staff, the two-pronged golden rings ring clearly): this depicts the dignity of his own travel on foot. Rulai baozhang qin zongji (the very traces of the Tathagata's jeweled staff): the Dharma-code (the rule) handed down in person by the Tathagata. The scripture says:
“The Buddha told the bhiksus: You should receive the staff. Why? Because the past Tathagatas and all the present Buddhas have held it.”
(See Master Hongde's Annotation to the Song of the Realization of the Way)
Not seeking the true, not cutting off the false, know that the two are empty and without marks.
No marks, no void, no non-void, this is the Tathagata's true mark.

Do not seek the true, do not cut off the false, and know that these two (seeking the true and cutting off the false) do not really exist, and so do not cling to their marks. Neither clinging to them as existing (no void), nor clinging to them as nonexistent (no non-void), this is the Middle Way (the true mark) that the Buddha teaches.

Bu qiu zhen, bu duan wang (not seeking the true, not cutting off the false): not seeking the true and not cutting off the false, but achieving that the five aggregates (form, feeling, thought, impulses, and consciousness) come and go like floating clouds, and the three poisons (greed, anger, and ignorance) rise and vanish like bubbles of water, this is the effort of the stage of free abiding. Ordinary people, whose effort in the stage of keeping is not yet accomplished, must seek the true and cut off the false. Otherwise it is “trying to run before one has learned to walk,” and the result is inevitably to speak of emptiness with the mouth while clinging to existence at every step, entangled without respite by the five aggregates and the three poisons. It is like a commoner who calls himself an emperor and must suffer the calamity of being put to death. Wu xiang (no marks)

: to be free of marks while in the midst of marks (not to cling to marks). For example, giving without clinging to marks is also called markless giving. In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch instructed:

“In this Dharma-gate, from the beginning onward, I first establish no-thought as the doctrine, no-marks as the essence, and no-abiding as the foundation. No-marks means to dwell among marks and yet be free of marks. No-thought means to dwell amid thought and yet be without thought.
