No-abiding is the original nature of people, which, amid the good and evil of the world, the fair and the ugly, and even amid enemies and kin, and at the time when words touch and sting, and cheating and contention arise, takes them all as empty, and does not think of requital, and amid each thought does not think of the former state.”
It also says:
“Being free from all marks outwardly is called no-marks. Being able to be free of marks, then the Dharma-essence is pure. This is taking no-marks as the essence.”
(For the annotations see
The Three Kinds of No-attempt
Wu kong wu bu kong (no void, no non-void): no void means that in the dream of ignorance there
is
this matter; and no non-void means that this matter is after all
nothing

(because this is a dream affair, and once the dream is over it is no more). Wu xiang wu kong wu bu kong (no marks, no void, no non-void): to have no marks toward no void and no non-void, that is, neither to cling to no void (existence) nor to cling to no non-void (nonexistence). Zhong dao (the Middle Way): not leaning toward existence, not leaning toward nonexistence, neither existing nor nonexistent, both existing and nonexistent, not falling into either extreme, perfectly harmonious and unobstructed, this is called the Middle Way.
The mind-mirror is bright, its reflection unobstructed, vast and brilliantly clear, pervading all the world-systems.
In the myriad forms arrayed, appearing in reflections, this single sphere of light is neither within nor without.

When the mind is pure, like a bright mirror, it reflects the myriad things without obstruction, and is bright and transparent, without the least obstruction, pervading the worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges. The myriad forms, dense as a forest, all appear reflected within it, and this single sphere of light (the wonderful, pure, bright mind) is neither within nor without.

Sha jie (the world of sands): worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges. Yi ke yuan guang fei nei wai (this single sphere of light is neither within nor without): the wonderful, pure, bright mind is neither within nor without. See in detail the passage “The Seven Places Where the Mind Was Sought” in the Surangama Sutra.
The reckless emptiness, denying cause and effect, and the vast, driftless wandering bring calamity.
Abandoning existence,
clinging to
emptiness is likewise a disease, like fleeing drowning and casting oneself into fire.

Recklessly clinging one-sidedly to emptiness (the reckless emptiness) and negating cause and effect (negating that there is cause and effect), rude and ignorant, brings calamity. Abandoning existence and clinging to emptiness is likewise a disease, like fleeing drowning and casting oneself into fire.

Bi ni er tou huo (fleeing drowning and casting oneself into fire): to avoid drowning and instead cast oneself into a pit of fire. This is a metaphor for the cultivator who, while abandoning existence, at the same time clings to emptiness. Clinging to existence and clinging to emptiness are both diseases; one should take the Middle Way.
Abandoning the false mind, taking up the true principle, a mind of taking and rejecting becomes a clever falseness.
The student who does not understand this and uses it for cultivation utterly mistakes the thief for his son.

Abandoning the false mind and taking up the true principle, a mind of taking and rejecting becomes a clever falseness. The student who does not understand this principle and uses it in cultivation truly takes the thief for his own son and robs his own family wealth.

She wang xin, qu zhen li (abandoning the false mind, taking up the true principle): “Abandoning the false mind and taking up the true principle” is the effort that must be done in the stage of keeping. But in the stage of free abiding, one must not abandon the false mind and not take up the true principle, but pursue the effortless practice, and must not use a mind of taking and rejecting to do the effort. Qiao wei (clever falseness): crafty (dishonest) and false.

Damaging the Dharma-wealth, destroying the merit, all comes from this mind, will, and consciousness; therefore the Chan gate finishes with the mind and suddenly enters the power of the vision and knowledge of the unborn.

Damaging the Dharma-wealth, destroying the merit, all is due to this consciousness-mind (the mind, will, and consciousness); therefore the Chan gate must be free of the mind, will, and consciousness in its contemplation (finishing with the mind), suddenly entering the power of the vision and knowledge of the unborn and undying.

Fa cai (the Dharma-wealth): the counterpart to “worldly wealth,” referring to the Buddha’s Dharma. Because the Buddha’s Dharma can nourish sentient beings and is the provision for nurturing their life of wisdom, as worldly treasure is, it is metaphorically called the Dharma-wealth. Sun fa cai (damaging the Dharma-wealth): causing the true Dharma not to appear before one. Mie gongde (destroying the merit): destroying the merit, at best one can only obtain blessings. For example, giving while clinging to marks only obtains the blessing of rebirth among the gods, and cannot escape the wheel of the six realms. Liao que xin (finishing with the mind): to make no use of the consciousness-mind (the mind, will, and consciousness). (On the consciousness-mind, see in detail the article
Mind, Self-nature, and Tathagata-garbha

) The mind, will, and consciousness: the collecting and accumulating is called mind; the reflecting and deliberating is called will; the distinguishing is called consciousness. Of the “mind, will, and consciousness,” the mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the alaya consciousness), the will to the seventh consciousness (the manas), and the consciousness to the remaining six (the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousnesses). “Mind, will, and consciousness,” then, constitute the eight consciousnesses of the consciousness-mind: the alaya, the manas, and the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousnesses. Li xin yishi can (contemplating apart from the mind, will, and consciousness): to investigate apart from the operation of the consciousness-mind (the mind, will, and consciousness). (See in detail
Contemplating Apart from the Mind, Will, and Consciousness

The great man wields the wisdom sword: the blade of prajna, the flame of the diamond; not only does it empty away the minds of the externalists, but it has long since cast down the courage of the heavenly devil.

The great man wields the wisdom sword (holding fast to the Diamond Sutra and cultivating according to it): the blade of prajna, the flame of the diamond. Not only does it destroy the evil minds of the externalists, but it has long since dashed the courage of the heavenly devil.

Da zhang fu (the great man): one with great resolve and great deeds, not limited to men. Bore feng xi jingang yan (the blade of prajna, the flame of the diamond): a metaphor for the Diamond Prajna Paramita Sutra (the Diamond Sutra, for short), which, like a sharp sword, cuts off all entanglements, and like a blazing flame, burns away afflictions and ignorance. Xi
(xi)
): a classical particle, equivalent to the modern “ah” or “alas.” For example: “The road is long and far, ah; I will seek up and down.”

Thundering the Dharma-thunder, beating the Dharma-drum, spreading the clouds of compassion and sprinkling the sweet dew; the dragons and elephants tramp, watering the boundless, and all of the three vehicles and five natures awaken.

Thundering the Dharma-thunder, beating the Dharma-drum, spreading the clouds of compassion, ah, and sprinkling the sweet dew; the dragons and elephants travel and patrol, watering the immeasurable beings, and all people of the three vehicles and five natures awaken.

Fa lei (the Dharma-thunder): the Buddha's Dharma is like thunder, able to startle and awaken the multitudes from their confusion. Long xiang (the dragons and elephants): the dragon and the elephant. Among the watery creatures the dragon is the mightiest, and among the land creatures the elephant is the mightiest, and so the dragon and the elephant are a metaphor for one who cultivates with great vigor and possesses great strength. Cu
(cu)

, ta (to tramp): to walk. San cheng (the three vehicles): the vehicle of the sravakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. Wu xing (the five natures): the capacities of all sentient beings can be divided into five classes, called the five natures: first, one who has the taintless seeds capable of cultivating the fruit of the arhat is called one of fixed nature as a sravaka. Second, one who has the taintless seeds capable of cultivating the fruit of the pratyekabuddha is called one of fixed nature as a pratyekabuddha. Third, one who has the taintless seeds capable of cultivating the fruit of Buddhahood is called one of fixed nature as a bodhisattva. Fourth, one who has two or three of the above taintless seeds, whose future stage of realization, when the conditions ripen, is not determined as to which fruit will be realized, is called one of indeterminate nature. Fifth, one who has none of the taintless seeds of the above three vehicles (the sravaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva vehicles), but only the defiled seeds capable of cultivating the fruit of humans and gods, is called one of no nature.
The snow-mountain's fat and sleek, all the more without mixture, purely yields the clarified milk which I always receive.
One nature, perfectly penetrating, penetrates all natures; one Dharma universally contains all dharmas.

The snow-mountain's “fat and sleek” (the name of a herb), all the more without the mixture of other weeds; after the white cow eats it, it purely yields the clarified milk (a metaphor for the one-vehicle Dharma) which I always take in. One nature (the Buddha-nature), perfectly penetrating, then all natures penetrate; one Dharma (the one-vehicle Dharma) universally contains all dharmas.

Xue shan fei ni (the snow-mountain's fat and sleek): on the snow-mountain there is a precious herb named fat and sleek, and the white cow eating it purely yields clarified milk. The Nirvana Sutra says:
“There is a herb on the snow-mountain, named ‘fat and sleek’; if the cow eats it, it purely gains clarified milk.”

Ti hu (clarified milk): milk products refined through many processes, first among all flavors, a metaphor for the supreme Buddha-Dharma. Yi cheng fa (the one-vehicle Dharma): the single teaching that can cause one to become a Buddha.
One moon universally appears in all the waters, and all the water-moons are gathered in the one moon.
The Dharma-bodies of all the Buddhas enter my nature, and my nature is wholly joined with the Tathagatas.

One round bright moon universally appears in all waters, and the reflections of the moon in all waters are all gathered and shone upon by this one round moon. The Dharma-bodies of all the Buddhas merge into my self-nature, and my self-nature wholly accords with all the Buddhas.
Tong gong (wholly together): together, in common.
One ground is complete with all grounds, neither form, nor mind, nor the karma of deeds.
In a snap of the fingers the eighty-thousand gates are completely accomplished, and in an instant the three great aeons are wiped away.

One ground (the Buddha-nature), perfectly penetrating, is complete with all grounds, and transcends body, mind, and activity (neither form, nor mind, nor the karma of deeds). In a single snap of the fingers, the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates are completely accomplished, and in an instant the three asamkhya aeons are wiped away (a metaphor for attaining Buddhahood on the spot).

Yi di (one ground): using the ground as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. Just as all the seeds of plants and trees grow relying on the ground, so all roots of goodness and merit grow relying on this Buddha-nature (one ground). Xing
(xing)

, ye (karma of deeds): the karma created by body, speech, and mind. San qi jie (the three great aeons): the three asamkhya aeons, which is the time for a bodhisattva to cultivate the Way and become a Buddha. Mie que san qi jie (wiping away the three great aeons): without needing the three asamkhya aeons, one attains Buddhahood on the spot.
It cannot be destroyed, it cannot be praised; the essence, like empty space, has no boundary.
It never leaves the present place, ever serene and still; to seek it, and you know you cannot see it.

Not to be destroyed, and not to be praised; the essence, like empty space, has no boundary. It never leaves the present place, ever serene and still; seek it, and you will know the (original nature) cannot be seen.
This paragraph describes the state in which the original nature manifests.

Ya an (the boundary): the edge. Mi ji zhi jun bu ke jian (seek it, and you will know you cannot see it): when the original nature manifests, it is in no-thought; to seek the original nature is to stir up a thought, and then the original nature is transformed again into the nature of consciousness.
It cannot be taken, it cannot be let go; in the unobtainable, just so it is obtained.
All words and phrases, and no words and phrases, what have they to do with my spiritual awakening?

(The original nature) cannot be taken, cannot be let go; in the unobtainable, just so it is obtained. All the discriminations of names and phrases, what have they to do with the awakening of my self-nature?
Qu bu de, she bu de, bu ke de zhong zhi (
zhi

) me de (it cannot be taken, it cannot be let go; in the unobtainable, just so it is obtained): it cannot be taken, cannot be let go; in the unobtainable, just so it is obtained. Taking and letting go both stir up a thought, and this cannot realize the original nature. When the effort is accomplished, one will taste the exquisiteness of the line “in the unobtainable, just so it is obtained,” and so it frequently appears in the recorded sayings of the Chan school.
Words and phrases, and no words and phrases
here
is a metaphor for the discrimination of names and phrases. “Words and phrases, and no words and phrases,”
is what the World-honored One spoke when he proclaimed the meaning of the hundred and eight phrases in the Lankavatara Sutra:
Real phrases, and no real phrases. Phrases of number, and no phrases of number.
(See in detail
Selected Annotations on the Lankavatara Sutra
) Si bian (discrimination): attempting to deduce reality from concepts.

blocks.text: Nine: The Great Gate of Giving

inline.s: In silence, he speaks; in speaking, he is silent; the gate of the great giving opens, with no obstruction
(yong)
or blockage.
If someone asks me what doctrine I understand,
I report: a guest of the great prajna.
In silence he speaks, and in speaking he is silent;
the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate (the great gate of giving) is opened
wide, with no impediment or stagnation. If someone asks me what doctrine I understand, I tell them: I alone cultivate and I alone proclaim the Dharma of the great prajna paramita.

Mo shi shuo (in silence he speaks): when there is no speech, he is expounding this perfect and sudden Dharma-gate (the great gate of giving). Wu yan er shuo (speaking without words): Subhuti sat in meditation in the cave (silent and still), and the gods rained down flowers in praise. The Venerable Subhuti asked: “Who is it raining flowers in praise in the sky?” A voice in the sky answered: “I am Brahma.” The Venerable asked: “Why do you praise?” Brahma said: “I revere the Venerable, who speaks well of the prajna paramita.” The Venerable said: “As to the prajna, I have not spoken a single word. Why should you praise it?” Brahma said: “The Venerable does not speak, and I do not hear. Not speaking and not hearing, this is truly speaking the prajna paramita.” Then again the earth quaked (the great earth trembled) and flowers rained down (like the descent of fresh flowers from the sky). (See the Continued Essential Sayings of the Ancient Worthies.) Shi shi mo (in speaking he is silent): while expounding the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate, one should grasp that profound meaning which is without words. Da shi men (the great gate of giving): refers to the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate transmitted by the Sixth Patriarch (the Dharma of the great prajna paramita). Because this is a Dharma-gate that causes one to reach Buddhahood directly without passing through the stages, it is an extremely great gift of Dharma, and so is called the great gate of giving. Mohe bore boluomi fa (the Dharma of the great prajna paramita): this is the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate transmitted by the Sixth Patriarch. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)
ascended the seat, and told the assembly: Purify the minds of all
(the assembly’s pure minds)
. Recollect the great prajna paramita.
The wisdom of bodhi and prajna, people of the world have it in themselves originally, only because
(only because)

the mind is deluded, they cannot awaken of themselves, and must rely on a great good teacher to point out and reveal the nature. Know that the foolish and the wise, the Buddha-nature originally has no distinction, only because of the difference in delusion and awakening, therefore there are the foolish and the wise. Now I will speak for you the
Dharma of the great prajna paramita
, making you all each gain wisdom.”

Mohe (maha): great. Bore (prajna): this is a transliteration of the Sanskrit, meaning wisdom, but this wisdom is not the cleverness and intelligence of the world, but the wonderful wisdom that sees clearly into the true reality of life and the universe, and is the right wisdom of the self-nature, and so it is kept as a transliteration. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter seventy-four, says:
“Prajna is the mother of all the Buddhas; abiding in this prajna, one can be complete with all the Buddha-dharmas.”

Boluomi duo (paramita): also translated as “parami,” meaning arriving at the other shore. Bore boluomi duo (prajna paramita): also translated as “prajna parami,” meaning to cross by the right wisdom of the self-nature to the shore of nirvana. Mohe bore ke (the guest of the great prajna):
one who alone cultivates and alone proclaims the Dharma of the great prajna paramita.
“Guest” here refers to one who devotes himself to a certain activity, for example, a swordsman, a knight-errant.
Either right or wrong, no one knows me; going along or going contrary, Heaven cannot fathom it. I long ago went through many aeons of cultivation, and I am no ordinary fellow come to deceive you.

Either approving (this as right) or disapproving (this as wrong), in truth none of them understand me; going along or going contrary (referring to the expedient skill in spreading the Dharma and in receiving and guiding students), Heaven too cannot fathom it. In the past I long ago cultivated through many aeons, and I am no ordinary fellow come to deceive you.
Setting up the Dharma-banner, establishing the essential doctrine, it is clearly the Buddha’s edict that
(chi
the same as “chi”)
Caoxi is.
First, Kasyapa first transmitted the lamp; in the twenty-eight generations of the Western heaven, the record.

Setting up the Dharma-banner, establishing the essential doctrine, and spreading the essential mind of the Buddha (the Buddha's edict) is the Sixth Patriarch Huineng (of Caoxi). This essential mind, Sakyamuni Buddha first transmitted to the Venerable Mahakasyapa, the founding patriarch of the Chan school. According to the record, the patriarchs of the Western heaven (ancient India) of the Chan school number twenty-eight in all.
Jian fa chuang
(chuang)

) (setting up the Dharma-banner): on the occasion of proclaiming the great Dharma, the banners are set up before the gate of the place of practice, and this is called the Dharma-banner. The Chan school, transferring its meaning, calls the unfolding and free expression of the Dharma the setting up of the Dharma-banner. Zong zhi (the essential doctrine): the principal purport of the scriptures, treatises, and the like. In the Chan school, the essential purport of Chan is called the essential doctrine. Chi
(chi)

) (edict): the same as “chi,” the command of an emperor. Cao xi (Caoxi): another name for the southern school of the Chan school, so named because the Sixth Patriarch Huineng proclaimed the Dharma at Baolin Monastery on Caoxi. Nan zong (the southern school): when Bodhidharma came to China to transmit Chan, by the time of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, there were two disciples, Huineng and Shenxiu; Huineng taught in the south of the Yangtze, and was called “the southern school,” while Shenxiu taught in the north, and was called “the northern school.”

Chuan deng (transmitting the lamp): transmitting the Dharma. The Buddha's Dharma is like a bright lamp, able to destroy the darkness of delusion, and so the transmission of the Dharma is called the transmission of the lamp. Di yi Kasyapa shou chuan deng (first, Kasyapa first transmitted the lamp): Sakyamuni Buddha first transmitted to the Venerable Mahakasyapa. The Sutra of Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve His Doubts says: The Brahma King came to Vulture Peak and offered a golden lotus flower to Sakyamuni Buddha, asking the Buddha to speak the Dharma. The World-honored One held up the flower and showed it to the assembly, and did not speak the Dharma. At the time, the million people of gods and humans all did not understand its meaning; only the Venerable Kasyapa broke into a smile. The World-honored One said: I have the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma, the wonderful mind of nirvana, the true form, which is formless, the subtle Dharma-gate, not established in words, transmitted apart from the teaching, and I entrust it to Mahakasyapa. This is the beginning of the Chan school. Zun zhe (the Venerable One): the honorific of an arhat. Zheng fa yan zang (the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma): the Buddha's mind-eye piercingly sees the true Dharma, called “the eye of the true Dharma,” and being deep and wide, containing the ten thousand virtues, is called “the treasury.” Zheng fa yan zang, niepan miao xin (the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma, the wonderful mind of nirvana): abbreviated as “the true Dharma and the wonderful mind,” that is, the profound, inconceivable truth realized by Sakyamuni Buddha; this state of great awakening is the profound, subtle Buddha-mind, which cannot be expressed or grasped through the teaching of words.

Er shi ba dai xi tian ji (the record of the twenty-eight generations of the Western heaven): the patriarchs of the Western heaven (ancient India) of the Chan school, according to the record, number twenty-eight: Sakyamuni Buddha first transmitted to the founding patriarch, the Venerable Mahakasyapa; the second patriarch, the Venerable Ananda; the third, the Venerable Sanavasa; the fourth, the Venerable Upagupta; the fifth, the Venerable Dhitaka; the sixth, the Venerable Micchaka; the seventh, the Venerable Vasumitra; the eighth, the Venerable Buddhanandi; the ninth, the Venerable Buddhamitra; the tenth, the Venerable Parsva; the eleventh, the Venerable Punyayasas; the twelfth, the great master Asvaghosha; the thirteenth, the Venerable Kapimala; the fourteenth, the great master Nagarjuna; the fifteenth, the Venerable Kanadeva; the sixteenth, the Venerable Rahulata; the seventeenth, the Venerable Sanghanandi; the eighteenth, the Venerable Gayasata; the nineteenth, the Venerable Kumarata; the twentieth, the Venerable Jayata; the twenty-first, the Venerable Vasubandhu; the twenty-second, the Venerable Manorhita; the twenty-third, the Venerable Haklenayasas; the twenty-fourth, the Venerable Simha; the twenty-fifth, the Venerable Basasita; the twenty-sixth, the Venerable Punyamitra; the twenty-seventh, the Venerable Prajnadhara; the twenty-eighth, the Venerable Bodhidharma. (See the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.)
The Dharma flowed east, entered this land, and Bodhidharma was the founding patriarch.
Six generations transmitted the robe, and all the world heard of it; the later ones who gained the Way, how can they be counted!

The great Dharma flowed eastward and entered this land, and Bodhidharma was the founding patriarch of the Chan school in China. Six generations transmitted the robe and bowl, and all the world knew of it; the later ones who gained the Way, how can they be counted (how can they be numbered)!

Chuan yi bo (transmitting the robe and bowl): from the first patriarch to the fifth, the Chan school transmitted the robe and bowl as a token of the transmission of the Dharma; after the Sixth Patriarch it was no longer transmitted. Later it also came to be used generally for the transmission of teaching from master to disciple. Liu dai (six generations): the first patriarch Bodhidharma, the second Huike, the third Sengcan, the fourth Daoxin, the fifth Hongren, and the sixth Huineng.

The true is not established, the false is originally void; having and non-being both cast aside, and not void and no void; the twenty gates of emptiness are originally without adherence; the one nature, the Tathagata-essence, is itself the same.

Not establishing the true, the false is originally void; having and non-being are both cast aside, with no void and no non-void; the twenty gates of emptiness are all without abiding; the ultimate essence of all the Buddhas (the one nature) is originally the same, without distinction from one another.

Zhen bu li (the true is not established): not establishing the true. “The true is not established” is an inverted construction, to strengthen the tone. Bu kong, kong (no void and void): the “no void and no non-void” spoken of above. No void is no non-void, and no non-void is void. Er shi kong (the twenty emptinesses): the twenty kinds of emptiness that express the principle that all dharmas are empty, from the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra

in the chapter on studying and contemplating. Namely: (1) inner emptiness, the six faculties of the inner dharmas — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — being impermanent and selfless, are empty. (2) outer emptiness, the six sense-objects of the outer dharmas — form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas — being impermanent and selfless, are empty. (3) the emptiness of both inner and outer, the six faculties and the six sense-objects all being empty. (4) the emptiness of emptiness, emptiness itself is again empty, that is, not clinging to all internal and external dharmas as empty, neither annihilated nor destroyed, the self-nature being thus. (5) great emptiness, the ten directions — east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below — all being empty. (6) supreme-meaning emptiness, the supreme nirvana being also empty. (7) conditioned emptiness, the conditioned realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm all being empty. (8) unconditioned emptiness, the unconditioned, without birth, abiding, change, and extinction, also being empty and not clung to. (9) the emptiness of ultimate emptiness, not clinging to all dharmas as ultimately unobtainable. (10) the emptiness of no limit, no beginning, middle, or end being obtainable, and no coming and going limit being obtainable, and not clinging to this. (11) the emptiness of dispersion, all dharmas being scattered and abandoned, being also empty. (12) the emptiness of no change, all dharmas being without scattering and abandonment, without change, this no-change also being empty and unobtainable. (13) the emptiness of inherent nature, all dharmas in their inherent nature, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are not made by the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the like, the inherent nature being originally empty. (14) the emptiness of self-marks, the self-marks of all dharmas, such as form's obstruction, feeling's reception, and the self-natures of thought, impulses, and consciousness, all being empty. (15) the emptiness of common marks, the common marks being all the emptiness of the unobtainable; as suffering is the common mark of the defiled dharmas, impermanence is the common mark of the conditioned dharmas, and emptiness and selflessness are the common marks of all dharmas. (16) the emptiness of all dharmas, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, with form and without form, with vision and without vision, with resistance and without resistance, defiled and undefiled, conditioned and unconditioned, and all such dharmas being empty, without clinging to them as empty. (17) the emptiness of the unobtainable, the dharmas of the three times all being unobtainable and not clung to. (18) the emptiness of no nature, no little nature being obtainable, which is no nature; this no nature being also unobtainable, therefore it is empty. (19) the emptiness of self-nature, the self-nature of the union of all dharmas having no substance, therefore it is empty. (20) the emptiness of no nature and self-nature, no nature and self-nature both being empty.

The mind is the root, dharmas are the dust; the two are like the traces and stains on a mirror; when the traces and stains are all removed, the light at last appears; when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, the nature is the true.

The mind is the root of afflictions, and dharmas are the dust of defilement; these two are like the traces and stains on a bright mirror; when the traces and stains are all removed, the bright light of the mirror then appears; when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, the nature of consciousness transforms into the original nature (true suchness).

Fa (dharmas): refers to all things. All things, whether large or small, with form or without form, are all called “dharmas.” Xin fa shuang wang xing ji zhen (when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, the nature is the true): when mind and dharmas are both forgotten, the self-nature is true suchness (the original nature).
Alas for the final Dharma, in this evil age, the beings have thin blessings, hard to tame and order.
Far from the sages, alas, false views are deep; the devil is strong and the Dharma weak, with much malice and harm.
Hearing of the Tathagata's sudden teaching-gate, they hate it and would not destroy it and break it to pieces.

Alas that it is now the period of the final Dharma, with the age turbid and evil, and the beings with thin blessings, hard to tame and order. Far from the Buddha, false views are deep; the evil devil is strong and the right Dharma weak, and they who spread the right Dharma are much attacked, slandered, and persecuted. As soon as they hear of the Tathagata's sudden teaching-gate, they hate it and wish it were destroyed and broken to pieces.
Far removed from the Sage: it has been a very long time since the Buddha was alive in the world.
Wrong wrought within the heart, calamity falls on the frame; no need to cry of grievance nor put the blame on another.
If you would not incur the karmic offenses of the unceasing hell, never slander the Tathagata's wheel of the true Dharma.

Wrong is wrought within the heart, and the calamitous retribution falls upon the body; this is all one's own doing and receiving, so there is no need to cry of grievance, and still less to blame another. If you would not incur the evil karma of the unceasing hell, then never slander the Tathagata's wheel of the true Dharma.
Lay the blame: to blame it on another.
In the woods of sandalwood stand no mingled trees; deep and dense and dark the lion takes his ease.
In the quiet forest he roams alone; far away the birds and beasts are flown.
The sandalwood forest has no mixed trees; deep, dense, and secluded the lion dwells there. In the tranquil forest he wanders alone, while birds and beasts all flee far away.
Sandal (
zhan
): that is, sandalwood. Lush and deep: the forest is thick and deep; the character here is the same as the one meaning "sinking", as "deep".
The lion cub, with all the throng behind, at three years old can roar a mighty sound.
If a wild beast pursues the Dharma king in strife, a hundred-year-old goblin chatters at life.

The lion cub has all the beasts following behind; by three years of age it can give a great roar. Those veteran purveyors of false beliefs (the wild jackals) contend against the Buddha's true Dharma, like a hundred-year-old goblin vainly opening its mouth to howl.

The lion cub: a metaphor for the advancing bodhisattva of sharp faculties, with the many following behind him. At three years old can give a great roar: the advancing bodhisattva of sharp faculties, having cultivated for no great length of time, can already expound the most supreme Mahayana (the great roar). Wild jackal (
han

): the meanest of all wild beasts. The wild jackal pursuing the Dharma king: a metaphor for those who preach error contending against the Buddha's true Dharma. "Pursuing" here means contending; for example, one says "contending for power". A hundred-year-old goblin vainly opening its mouth: "vainly" means to no purpose.
The perfect and sudden teaching
knows no
favoritism; if a doubt will not be settled, at once one must contend.
It is not that this mountain monk parades himself and others; it is lest in your practice you fall into the pit of annihilation and of eternalism.

The perfect and sudden teaching does not indulge human feeling; if there is a doubt unsettled, then one must debate it until it is clear. It is not that I would assert myself to win a personal contest of losing or winning; it is only for fear that in your practice you may fall into the trap of the view of annihilation and the view of eternalism.

The two views of annihilation and eternalism: the view of annihilation and the view of eternalism. The view of annihilation is the heterodox view insisting that after death the body and mind are cut off and there is no further rebirth; the view of eternalism is the heterodox view insisting that body and mind are permanent and never extinguished.
Not-not is not, and is is not the is; an error of a hair's breadth takes you a thousand miles astray.
If right, the Dragon Girl at once becomes a Buddha; if wrong, the Good Star falls while still in life.

Not is not, and is is; an error of a hair's breadth is a loss of a thousand miles. If correct, then the Dragon Girl at once becomes a Buddha; if wrong, then Good Star falls headlong into the unceasing hell in this very body.

An error of a hair's breadth, a loss of a thousand miles: though at the outset the deviation is ever so slight, the outcome as it develops is a vast error. The Dragon Girl's becoming a Buddha: the eight-year-old Dragon Girl, through the merit of upholding the Lotus Sutra, becomes a Buddha in that very body. Good Star: the son born to Shakyamuni Buddha while he was still the crown prince. After he left home, he cut off the afflictions of the realm of desire and attained the fourth dhyana. But later, by associating with evil companions, he lost the liberation he had gained, and then held that there was no Dharma of nirvana, gave rise to the heterodox view denying cause and effect, and even conceived an evil mind toward the Buddha, so that in that very life he fell into the unceasing hell.
In my early years I piled up learning, and also sought out commentaries and searched the sutras and treatises.
Distinguishing names and marks I knew no rest, like counting sand at the sea's bottom, laboring only to trap myself.

In my youth I heaped up learning, and also explored commentaries and pored over the sutras and treatises. Without rest, I applied myself to sorting out the names and marks (seeking only understanding, not rising from understanding into practice
, from practice attaining realization
), just as
one who reaches the bottom of the sea and, instead of taking the treasure, counts the grains of sand
, only to trap oneself in vain.

Master Shenhui is telling of how in his early years he too took a roundabout road. Had he not repented in time, he too would have erred by a hair's breadth and lost a thousand miles, and squandered a whole lifetime.

Names and marks: the terms and phrases of Buddhism. Counting sand at the sea's bottom: reaching the bottom of the sea and, instead of taking the treasure, counting the grains of sand. This is to say that in exploring the commentaries and studying the sutras and treatises, one should use the finger pointing at the moon and see the moon by following the finger (rising from understanding into practice, and through practice attaining realization). If one puts all one's energy into sorting out and studying names and marks, that is taking the finger that points at the moon as the moon itself and working on it, and so one falls onto a wrong path. The ancient worthy warns: one should use the finger to see the moon, and must not take the finger for the moon.

Yet I was sternly rebuked by the Tathagata: what benefit is there in counting another's treasures? Ever stumbling on the path of awakening, I sought in vain; for many years I toiled as a guest in the dust.

Again and again I was severely reproved by the Buddha; of what benefit to oneself is counting another's treasures (from morn to night counting another's treasures, yet having not half a coin of one's own)? Ever stumbling along the path of awakening (the bodhi way) and walking in vain, for many years I needlessly traveled about in the wind and dust, going from one teacher to another.
What benefit is there in counting another's treasures: the sutras, treatises, and commentaries are all guides for practice. If one does not apply them to one's own practice and put them into action,
then one is "counting another's treasures from morn to night, yet having not half a coin of one's own"; what benefit is that to oneself?
Stumbling (
ceng
): to be beset by hardships.
With a skewed nature, one misreads understanding, and fails to reach the Tathagata's perfect and sudden design.
The two vehicles are diligent but lack the mind of the Way; the heterodox are clever but have no wisdom.

With skewed faculties and mistaken understanding, one cannot comprehend the Tathagata's perfect and sudden Dharma-door. Though the two vehicles are diligent, they lack the mind of bodhi; though the heterodox are clever, they lack the wisdom of liberation.
Nature and faculties: the various natures and faculties. Bodhi: the wisdom that cuts off all afflictions and ignorance and realizes nirvana.

Also foolish, also dull and doting, upon an empty fist they build a real understanding; taking the finger for the moon, they labor in vain, and in the sphere of roots and objects forge all manner of fancies.

Foolish too, and dull and silly, they take real understanding to be born upon an empty fist (the expedient sayings), and, falsely clinging to the finger pointing at the moon as the bright moon, waste their effort; in the sphere of the roots, the dusts, and the dharmas (the five aggregates, the twelve sense-fields, and the eighteen elements) they vainly fancy and conjecture.
Dotting (
ai
): foolish, without knowledge.
Empty fist: to make a fist of an empty hand to startle children; a metaphor for the expedient sayings used to skillfully subdue sentient beings. The Ratnakuta Sutra says:

"As with an empty fist one lures a child, showing it a promise of something to make it glad, then opening the hand and finding nothing, the child thereupon wails again. So too the Buddhas, inconceivable, skillfully subdue the sort of sentient beings, knowing that the nature of things has no existence, and by provisional names set up and display them in the world."
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
"When I sat at the place of enlightenment, wisdom was not to be had. With an empty fist one beguiles children, so as to save them all."

The finger pointing at the moon: the finger that points out the moon. The finger pointing at the moon is the finger that indicates the moon. Buddhism likens "true thusness" to the "moon", so for those who do not know true thusness (the moon), it uses various dharmas (the finger pointing at the moon) to explain true thusness (the moon). The finger pointing at the moon is a metaphor for the various dharmas spoken by the Buddha, that is, the eighty-four thousand Dharma-doors and the more than five thousand fascicles of scriptures. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
The sutra teachings
(all the scriptural teachings)
, are like the finger pointing at the moon. If one then sees the moon, one knows that what was pointed at was after all not the moon
(one then knows that the finger is after all not the moon)

Sutra: translated into Chinese as "connecting scripture", the general name for all the Buddha-dharma. "Connecting" is to connect above with the wonderful principle of all Buddhas and connect below with the faculties of sentient beings. "Scripture" means warp-threads, stringing the meaning together so that it is not scattered; it also means canonical text. Roots, objects, and dharmas: the five aggregates, twelve sense-fields, and eighteen elements. Five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Twelve sense-fields: the six external objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) and the six internal faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). Eighteen elements: the six objects, six faculties, and six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness).
Not seeing a single dharma, that is the Tathagata; only then may one be called the Lord of Contemplation.
Awakened, the obstructions of karma are originally empty; not yet awakened, one must repay the debt from a former life.

Seeing no dharma as real, one is the Tathagata; only then is one called the Lord of Contemplation (Avalokiteshvara). Realizing the unborn dharmas, the obstructions of karma are originally empty; while one has not yet realized, one must still repay the debts of a former life.
Not seeing a single dharma, that is the Tathagata: "not seeing a single dharma" means not taking any single dharma as real and clinging to its mark. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All marks are false and vain."
It also says:
"To be free of all marks is to be called all the Buddhas."
The Three-Part Service of Zhongfeng says:
"The Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the unborn; sentient beings, within the serene and unborn, see only arising and ceasing."
Lord of Contemplation:
in the realm where things and principle are unobstructed, one contemplates and reaches freedom. The Sixth Patriarch says:
"Originally not a single thing; where could dust alight?"
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). Debt (
su
): the karmic debt of a former lifetime.

Hungry, one meets the royal banquet and cannot eat; sick, one meets the king of physicians and how shall one be cured? Practicing meditation within the realm of desire is the power of the unborn view; the lotus born in fire at last is not destroyed.
The brave giver, having transgressed, awakens to the unborn, and of old became a Buddha, and is here now.]

Hungry, yet meeting the royal feast and not eating, how can one be filled? Sick, yet meeting the king of physicians and not taking the medicine, how can one be healed? Practicing meditation within the sphere of desire is due to the power of the unborn view, like the red lotus that springs up in fire and is never harmed. The Bhikshu Yongshi (Brave Giver), though he had violated the two grave precepts of lust and killing, because he realized the patience of the unborn, long ago became a Buddha, named the Tathagata Precious Moon, and is here still.
Cured (
chai
): healed of illness.
The brave giver, having transgressed, awakens to the unborn, and of old became a Buddha, and is here now:
(The Bhikshu Yongshi had a secret affair with a woman and poisoned her husband,)

and his mind was filled with great remorse: "I have practiced the dharma of lust and also taken a human life. Alas! How strange! I am now a denizen of hell." At that time there was a bodhisattva named Nasikun
ju

tara, who said to Yongshi: "Bhikshu, do not fear; I now have the power to give you fearlessness." He thereupon entered the samadhi of the precious seal, and from his body produced innumerable Buddhas, who all in one voice spoke this verse: "All dharmas are like images in a mirror, and also like the moon in water; ordinary beings, with deluded minds, discriminate between folly, hatred, and love." The Bhikshu Yongshi, seeing the miraculous transformations of these transformation-Buddhas, reflected and chose among all dharmas, left all the covers and entanglements, and realized the patience of the unborn. Now he has become a Buddha, in the west, at a distance measured by the sands of the Ganges from this buddha-land; there is a land named Constant Light, and the Buddha is named the Tathagata Precious Moon."
(The Sutra of Purifying Karmic Obstructions)

Covers and entanglements: the five covers and ten entanglements. Five covers: five kinds of afflictions. "Cover" is another name for affliction, because afflictions cover over people's mind-nature so that wholesome dharmas do not arise. The five covers are: greed, anger, sloth-and-sleep, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt. Restlessness-and-remorse: restlessness and remorse; both of these states make the mind unable to be at peace and give rise to affliction. Restlessness: the waves of thought that cannot be gathered in. Ten entanglements: ten kinds of afflictions. "Entanglement" is another name for affliction, because afflictions tie up the body and mind of sentient beings so that they cannot escape birth and death or realize nirvana. The ten entanglements are: shamelessness, lack of self-respect, jealousy, stinginess, remorse, sloth-and-sleep, restlessness, sluggishness, anger, and concealment (hiding one's own wrongdoing).
The lion's roar, the fearless teaching, I deeply sigh for the muddled and stubborn who only know that grave offenses obstruct bodhi, and see not the secret instruction opened by the Tathagata.
The lion's roar, the fearless teaching; I deeply lament (
jie
) those muddled fellows who only know that grave offenses obstruct bodhi, and yet do not see the secret of liberation revealed by the Tathagata.

The lion's roar: the Buddha's preaching of the Dharma sounds through the ten directions, and all the hosts of Mara are subdued, just as when a lion roars all the hundred beasts are cowed. Fearless teaching: the Buddha speaks in the midst of the assembly, calm and without fear. Muddled (
meng
): confused. Stubborn (
da
): a description of those who, thick and hard like cowhide, are stubborn and do not understand principle.
Two bhikshus violated lust and killing; Upali's firefly-light added to their guilt; the great Vimalakirti at once dissolved their doubt, like the blazing sun melting the frost and snow.

There were two bhikshus who violated the two grave precepts of lust and killing; the admonition of the Venerable Upali, like the firefly's light, only increased the burden of their guilt; the great Vimalakirti taught them repentance through real marks and at once dispelled their doubt, just as the red sun dissolves the frost and snow.

Two bhikshus violated lust and killing, Upali's firefly-light added to their guilt, the great Vimalakirti at once dissolved their doubt: There were two bhikshus dwelling in the mountains, in a small hut, cultivating. One bhikshu went out, and the other fell asleep. A wood-gathering woman, taking advantage of the sleeping bhikshu, secretly committed lust with him. When the bhikshu woke he was filled with great remorse. The bhikshu who had gone out returned to the hut and was told of this. Hearing it, he flew into a rage and went in search of the woman to teach her a lesson. The woman was frightened and fled, and in her panic stumbled and fell into a deep pit and died. These two bhikshus, deeply feeling their offense, went together to the Venerable Upali to seek repentance. The Venerable's admonition only made them the more distressed. The great Vimalakirti, learning of it, upbraided the Venerable Upali, saying: "You should not disturb their minds and increase their offense; rather you should teach them how to put it away. You must know that the nature of offense is not within, not without, and not in between. Where there is a defiled mind there are defiled sentient beings; where there is a pure mind there are pure sentient beings. Where there is delusion there is defilement on the mind; where there is no delusion the mind is pure. All dharmas are false views, empty and unreal, born from delusion. Offense arises from the mind; one should repent it from the mind; when the defilement of the mind is extinguished, the offense too is extinguished." The two bhikshus, hearing this, at once had their doubt and remorse dispelled, and awakened to the unsurpassed mind of the Way. (See the Vimalakirti Nirdeśa Sutra

Offense arises from the mind, and one should repent it with the mind; when the mind is gone the offense too is gone; both mind and offense gone, both empty — this is called true repentance."
The Vimalakirti Nirdeśa Sutra says:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
The Sutra of Contemplating Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:
"All the oceans of karmic obstruction arise from delusion. If one would repent, sit upright and contemplate the real mark. All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can melt them away."

The Sutra on the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle says:
"If one can repent in accord with the Dharma, all afflictions are entirely removed; as a conflagration at the end of an age destroys the world, burning up Mount Sumeru and the great seas."
Inconceivable, the power of liberation, whose wondrous functions are numberless as the sands of the Ganges and without limit.

How dare I begrudge the toil of the four offerings; even ten thousand taels of gold can be received. Broken body and crushed bones are not enough to repay, but one line understood at once surpasses a hundred billion.

Inconceivable, the power of liberation through the unborn; its many wondrous functions, as countless as the sands of the Ganges, have no limit. How dare I decline the toil of making the four offerings; even ten thousand taels of gold can be borne with ease. To smash the body and crush the bones would not be enough to repay the Buddha's great kindness; a single line clearly understood at once leaps beyond hundreds of billions of eons of gradual progression.

The four offerings: to make offerings with the four kinds of requisites: food, clothing, bedding, and medicine. Even ten thousand taels of gold can be received: even the offering of ten thousand taels of gold can be borne with ease. The Essential Instructions on Cultivating the Mind says:

"If one awakens to this mind, truly it is what is called treading no ladder but directly mounting the ground of Buddhahood, transcending the three realms at every step, and returning home, at once severing all doubt. One then becomes the teacher of gods and humans, with compassion and wisdom mutually supporting, fulfilled in the twofold benefit, and worthy of the offerings of gods and humans, daily consuming ten thousand taels of gold. If you are thus, you are truly a great man, and the great work of a life is done."
(Translation:

If you awaken to this mind of empty stillness and numinous knowing, it is truly what is called treading no ladder but directly mounting the ground of Buddhahood, at every step transcending the three realms, and at once severing the doubt of whether one can return home (become a Buddha). You can then be the teacher of gods and humans, with compassion and wisdom mutually sustaining, fulfilled in the twofold benefit of self and others, able to receive the offerings of gods and humans, daily bearing the offering of ten thousand taels of gold. If you are like this, you are truly a great man, and the great work of a lifetime is done.

Mutually sustaining: to support one another. The twofold benefit: self-benefit and benefiting others. Seeking above the buddha-fruit is self-benefit; transforming sentient beings below is benefiting others. Daily consuming ten thousand taels of gold: this shows the vastness of merit and virtue. The old master of Guishan says:
"This old monk, once seated in meditation, can consume ten thousand taels of gold (
means he is worthy of bearing the offering of ten thousand taels of gold)
The ancient worthy says:
"If the venerable one has truly awakened, then turning the great earth into gold and churning the long river into buttermilk to offer the venerable one is not out of place
(to offer these to the venerable one is what is deserved)
. But if not, then for a single grain of rice or a single thread, one must drag the plow and haul the rake to repay it before one is done."
(From the Commentary on the Song of Enlightenment by the Virtuous Hongde)

One line understood at once surpasses a hundred billion: one line clearly understood at once leaps beyond hundreds of billions of eons of gradual progression. "One line" is the line in the Diamond Sutra:
"To be free of all marks is to be called all the Buddhas."
The king of dharmas, the highest and most supreme, to which the Tathagatas countless as the sands of the Ganges all together bear witness.
I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; those who believe and receive it all attain response.

The perfect and sudden Dharma-door is the king of dharmas, highest and most supreme; the Tathagatas countless as the sands of the Ganges all together bear witness to it. I now have penetrated this wish-fulfilling jewel (the perfect and sudden Dharma-door); those who believe and receive it will all be in accord.
[Clearly and distinctly see: not a single thing, no person either, and no Buddha. The thousand-great-thousand worlds are but a bubble on the sea; all sages and saints are like lightning in the sky.]

Clearly and distinctly one sees that there is no thing, no person, and also no Buddha. The countless worlds, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like a bubble on the sea's surface; all sages and saints are like a flash of lightning in the empty sky.
Sands of worlds: worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges. Bubble (
ou
): a water bubble.
This passage is the realm of one who has realized the unborn dharmas. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"Perfect enlightenment universally shines, quiescent and nondual, and within it the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions of asamkhyeyas and inconceivable numbers of buddha-worlds, countless as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising and falling in confusion."

[The sun may be made cold, the moon may be made hot; the hosts of Mara cannot destroy this true teaching. The elephant's carriage climbs the towering peak with slow advance; who has ever seen a mantis able to stop its wheel

The sun may be made cold and the moon made hot, but the hosts of Mara cannot destroy the true teaching of the perfect and sudden. The elephant king's carriage advances slowly along the steep and towering peaks; who has ever seen a mantis able to block it?

The elephant's carriage: the carriage of the elephant king, a metaphor for the perfect and sudden Dharma-door. Towering peak: a high and steep peak, a metaphor for the dangerous turbid world. Wheel-tracks: the fixed route along which a carriage runs.

[The great elephant does not roam the rabbit's path; great awakening is not bound by petty details. Do not, with the view from a tube, slander the vast sky; if you are not yet enlightened, this is now my formula for you!]

The great elephant does not walk the small path of the rabbit; great awakening is not tied down by trifling details. Do not use your shallow opinion (the view from a tube) to slander the vast and profound sudden teaching. If you are not yet enlightened, then this Song of Enlightenment of mine is the secret formula guiding you!

The view from a tube: a shallow opinion, like looking at the sky through a tube, where the range seen is very small. Slandering the vast sky by the view from a tube: looking at the sky through a tube and saying the blue sky is only as wide as the tube's diameter. This is a metaphor for those who are not yet enlightened and vainly slander the sudden teaching with their own shallow opinions.
